The world-view (loka-siddhānta) is taught because the triple world is a burning house, and thus there is fear;
the person-view (pudgala-siddhānta) is taught because it gives rise to goodness, and thus there is joy;
the therapeutic view (pratipakṣa-siddhānta) is taught because it severs evil, and thus there is weary detachment.
By teaching the *paramārtha-siddhānta*, one realizes the truth and thereby severs doubt.
Furthermore, by teaching the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), one feels dread;
by teaching the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), one feels joy.
By teaching the Truth of Origination, one develops weary detachment;
by teaching the Truth of the Path, one severs doubt. Regarding the term "prostration" (kai-shou), Zheng Xuan says: [text follows].
*Kai* (稽) means "to reach";
it refers to bowing the body down until the hands touch the ground to manifest reverence.
*Shilì* (十力) refers to the ten kinds of intellectual power of the Tathāgata.
First is the power of knowledge regarding what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*).
This is the knowledge that determines cause and effect;
that is to say, when the principle of cause and effect is consistent, it is called "possible" (*sthāna*).
That which is inconsistent is called "impossible" (*asthāna*).
Second is the power of karma, which is the knowledge of the distinctions between the karmas of the three realms and six destinies. Third is the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
That is to say, because one knows all meditative concentrations and has attained mastery over them;
the power of the faculties, which knows the superior, middling, and inferior faculties of all sentient beings;
and the power of the five desires.
Knowing that the inclinations and desires of all sentient beings differ,
there are six powers of nature,
also called the powers of the elements (*dhātu*).
This refers to knowing the distinctions among various natures.
Seventh is the power regarding the path;
"path" refers to the cause, "place" to the basis, and "fruit" to the result—meaning one knows that by practicing the cause, one attains the fruit.
Eighth is the power of recollecting past lives,
by which one knows the distinctions in the lifespans received in previous births.
Ninth is the power of the divine eye.

The tenth is the power of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-bala*), because it knows the dharmas free from outflows (*anāsrava*). This is due to knowing the causes and conditions of birth and death.
This is the general name for "power" (*bala*).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Thorough knowledge that is ultimate is called power."
According to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, the power consists in unimpeded thorough knowledge;
according to the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*, it consists in being unsubdued, unbending, unsurpassed, and immovable.
Regarding the "fearlessnesses," these are the four fearlessnesses.
First, the fearlessness of omniscience:
he declares himself to be endowed with all-knowledge.
Second, the fearlessness of the destruction of the outflows.
He himself declares that all his outflows of affliction have been exhausted and that he possesses fearlessness regarding the three obstacles to the Path;
yet he himself says, "I recognize that the afflictions of greed and desire can obstruct the Noble Path."
The fearlessness regarding the path leading out of suffering:
he declares of himself, "I know the untainted path capable of bringing about liberation from birth and death.
Because he teaches these four dharmas in the midst of the great assembly with a heart free from timidity, he possesses fearlessness.
Second, regarding the clarification of the mode of activity:
as stated in the Sūtra,
the non-Buddhists raise an objection, saying:
If he possessed all-encompassing knowledge (*sarvajñā*),
why did he ask the bhikṣus whether almsfood was easy to obtain and so forth?
The Buddha replied:
"It is not that I do not know;
however, I ask in accordance with the tradition of the Master and his disciples.
[The second objection states:]..."
"If he has exhausted all outflows,
for what reason did the Buddha revile Devadatta and speak with loving words to Rāhula?
The Buddha replied:
It is appropriate that things be thus regulated;
it is not a matter of afflictions or outflows (*āsrava*).
Regarding this, the three objections state:
Regarding the statement that "desire hinders the path," why is it that those who have attained the first two fruits still experience the five desires?
The Buddha replied:
"Because [desire] definitely hinders the attainment of the latter two fruits."
The fourth objection states:
"Gautama, you say that the Eightfold Noble Path can lead one out of suffering.
For what reason, then, do Arhats still experience cold, heat, hunger, thirst, and so forth?"
The Buddha said:
"The Noble Path is indeed truly able to exhaust suffering;
it is simply that the Arhat's residual retribution has not yet perished."
These latter two forms of fearlessness are here explained according to the Hīnayāna;
in reality, however, they are unsurpassed.
To realize the Great Way, one must fundamentally be free from all afflictions.
It is not the knowledge of the two or four fruits [of the śrāvaka].
Furthermore, the Dharmakāya, being the nature of True Suchness (tathatā), is without arising or ceasing; because it does not arise from the four great elements, it is "liberation from suffering.
It is not like the liberation from suffering of the Two Vehicles, which occurs at the final body after the exhaustion of fetters and karma. [This is] the eighteen unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma).
First, no lapse in physical conduct;
second, no lapse in verbal conduct;
third, no lapse in mental conduct.
Fourth, there is no lack of mental stability; fifth, there is no lack of discernment of characteristics;
sixth, there is no relinquishment without prior knowledge.
Seventh, his desire does not diminish.
Eighth, his mindfulness does not diminish.
Ninth, his diligence does not diminish.
10. No diminution of wisdom;
11. no diminution of liberation;
12. no diminution of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Twelfth, bodily action follows wisdom;
fourteenth, action is wisdom;
fifteenth, mental action follows wisdom.
Sixteenth, wisdom that knows the past;
seventeenth, wisdom that knows the future;
eighteenth, wisdom that knows the present.
Among these, the first six involve severing the faults of body, speech, and mind,
remaining eternally in a concentrated state of mind, maintaining equanimity toward enemies and kin,
and relinquishing things with full awareness.
The next six are virtues:
namely, the perfection of desire, mindfulness, diligence, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, being complete and without deficiency.
The final six are wisdom.
This refers to the three types of action and the three periods of time being eternally abiding in right wisdom without forgetfulness.
As for the term "unshared" (*āveṇika*),
it means that when the Buddha dwells in this Dharma, he does not share it with ordinary beings or those of the two vehicles.
Furthermore, both the *Ratnakūṭa* and the *Mahāsaṃnipāta* sūtras state that the three types of action being without fault constitutes the first [perfection];
adding the absence of contention constitutes the second;
and the absence of forgetfulness or error constitutes the third.
The remainder is the same as before.
The "Chapter on the Buddha-land" is like a king proclaiming a righteous edict;
the nine chapters from the "Chapter on Expedient Means" downward are like the administration of affairs by a great minister.
The morning after the completion of the two chapters on the Bodhisattva’s practice and the vision of Akṣobhya is the venerable category [of the ultimate].
"Empty and devoid of image" means that the Dharma-body is empty and lacks any form or image. "Form has no permanent substance" means...
Sometimes manifesting as sixteen feet tall,
sometimes manifesting as a thousand feet tall;
with long lifespans or short lifespans.

The response to beings is impermanent and empty. Since the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) is itself impermanent in its size, its substance responds to beings; likewise, its manifestations are not constant in being pure or defiled, nor fixed in location. As for the statement that "beauty and ugliness belong to them [the beings]," it means: [The response-body] manifests according to the capacity of the beings to be saved, appearing as either beautiful or ugly. It is like a reflection in a mirror: when the mirror is clear, the reflection appears beautiful; when the mirror is turbid, the reflection appears ugly. Thus, the beauty or ugliness belongs to the beings themselves. Furthermore, the response-body manifests in accordance with the beings' karmic conditions, appearing in various forms such as those of gods, humans, or animals. Therefore, the distinction between beauty and ugliness belongs to the beings. Moreover, the response-body manifests in accordance with the beings' mental dispositions, appearing as either beautiful or ugly. Just as a single moon reflects in many waters, appearing beautiful or ugly depending on the clarity or turbidity of the water, so too does the response-body manifest in accordance with the beings' mental dispositions; thus, the distinction between beauty and ugliness belongs to the beings. Furthermore, the response-body manifests in accordance with the beings' faculties, appearing as either beautiful or ugly. Just as a single lamp illuminates many rooms, appearing bright or dim depending on the state of the rooms, so too does the response-body manifest in accordance with the beings' faculties; thus, the distinction between beauty and ugliness belongs to the beings. Finally, the response-body manifests in accordance with the beings' aspirations, appearing as either beautiful or ugly. Just as a single drum produces various sounds according to how it is struck, so too does the response-body manifest in accordance with the beings' aspirations; thus, the distinction between beauty and ugliness belongs to the beings. This is what is meant by "beauty and ugliness belong to them. Regarding "and so forth," it refers to the fact that the response-body manifests in accordance with the beings' afflictions, appearing as either beautiful or ugly. Just as a single medicine cures various illnesses, appearing effective or ineffective depending on the illness, so too does the response-body manifest in accordance with the beings' afflictions; thus, the distinction between beauty and ugliness belongs to the beings. Furthermore, the response-body manifests in accordance with the beings' roots of goodness, appearing as either beautiful or ugly. Just as a single sun shines upon many lands, appearing radiant or obscured depending on the land, so too does the response-body manifest in accordance with the beings' roots of goodness; thus, the distinction between beauty and ugliness belongs to the beings. Additionally, the response-body manifests in accordance with the beings' past causes and conditions, appearing as either beautiful or ugly. Just as a single echo follows various sounds, appearing loud or faint depending on the sound, so too does the response-body manifest in accordance with the beings' past causes and conditions; thus, the distinction between beauty and ugliness belongs to the beings. Moreover, the response-body manifests in accordance with the beings' present circumstances, appearing as either beautiful or ugly. Just as a single cloud covers many mountains, appearing dense or thin depending on the mountain, so too does the response-body manifest in accordance with the beings' present circumstances; thus, the distinction between beauty and ugliness belongs to the beings. Furthermore, the response-body manifests in accordance with the beings' future destinies, appearing as either beautiful or ugly. Just as a single seed grows into various fruits, appearing sweet or bitter depending on the fruit, so too does the response-body manifest in accordance with the beings' future destinies; thus, the distinction between beauty and ugliness belongs to the beings. Finally, the response-body manifests in accordance with the beings' ultimate liberation, appearing as either beautiful or ugly. Just as a single path leads to various destinations, appearing pleasant or difficult depending on the destination, so too does the response-body manifest in accordance with the beings' ultimate liberation; thus, the distinction between beauty and ugliness belongs to the beings. This is what is meant by "and so forth. This concludes the explanation of the response-body. Next, we shall explain the Dharma-body. The Dharma-body is eternally quiescent and non-arising; it transcends all phenomena and is beyond verbal expression. It is the true nature of all dharmas, which is originally unborn and unceasing. It is neither existent nor non-existent, neither one nor many, neither coming nor going, neither born nor dying. It is the realm of the Buddhas, the treasury of the Tathāgatas, the source of all wisdoms, and the foundation of all virtues. It is inconceivable, ineffable, and beyond the reach of thought. It is only through the power of the Buddhas that it can be slightly indicated. It is like the great ocean: though it is vast and deep, it cannot be measured; though it contains all jewels, they cannot be exhausted. It is like space: though it pervades all things, it has no form; though it accommodates all phenomena, it is never filled. It is like a great mirror: though it reflects all images, it has no discrimination; though it is always present before all beings, it has no attachment. It is like a great drum: though it produces various sounds, it has no intention; though it awakens all beings, it has no effort. It is like a great cloud: though it rains everywhere, it has no partiality; though it moistens all lands, it has no exhaustion. It is like a great fire: though it burns all fuel, it has no end; though it consumes all afflictions, it has no residue. It is like a great wind: though it moves all things, it has no obstruction; though it shakes all worlds, it has no fatigue. It is like a great mountain: though it supports all beings, it is immovable; though it endures all kalpas, it is indestructible. It is like a great river: though it flows continuously, it has no interruption; though it carries all beings across, it has no weariness. It is like a great physician: though he cures all illnesses, he has no pride; though he bestows the medicine of Dharma, he has no expectation. It is like a great teacher: though he instructs all disciples, he has no favoritism; though he reveals the path of truth, he has no concealment. It is like a great king: though he rules all realms, he has no desire; though he enjoys the bliss of Dharma, he has no attachment. It is like a great treasure: though it satisfies all seekers, it is inexhaustible; though it fulfills all wishes, it is without depletion. It is like a great light: though it illuminates all darkness, it is without limit; though it dispels all ignorance, it is without cessation. It is like a great vessel: though it holds all dharmas, it is without leakage; though it contains all wisdoms, it is without outflow. It is like a great bridge: though it spans all worlds, it is without decay; though it leads all beings to the other shore, it is without wear. It is like a great net: though it catches all beings, it is without discrimination; though it gathers all into the Great Vehicle, it is without exclusion. It is like a great palace: though it houses all Bodhisattvas, it is without boundaries; though it is the abode of all sages, it is without center. It is like a great garden: though it nurtures all roots of goodness, it is without season; though it brings forth all flowers of merit, it is without end. It is like a great field: though it yields all fruits of virtue, it is without harvest; though it ripens all sentient beings, it is without exhaustion. It is like a great mirror: though it reflects all phenomena, it is without image; though it manifests all Buddhas, it is without form. It is like a great void: though it encompasses all dharmas, it is without substance; though it accommodates all beings, it is without location. It is like a great emptiness: though it is the source of all dharmas, it is without birth; though it is the mother of all Buddhas, it is without origin. It is like a great tranquility: though it pacifies all afflictions, it is without effort; though it extinguishes all suffering, it is without cessation. It is like a great liberation: though it releases all beings, it is without bondage; though it grants the freedom of Nirvana, it is without attainment. It is like a great awakening: though it awakens all minds, it is without thought; though it realizes the Way, it is without realization. It is like a great equality: though it treats all beings equally, it is without partiality; though it views all dharmas as identical, it is without discrimination. It is like a great compassion: though it embraces all beings, it is without attachment; though it pities all who suffer, it is without weariness. It is like a great joy: though it delights in the Dharma, it is without craving; though it rejoices in liberation, it is without pride. It is like a great equanimity: though it remains impartial toward all, it is without indifference; though it dwells in the Middle Way, it is without extremes. It is like a great vow: though it aspires to save all, it is without limit; though it seeks the Buddha-way, it is without end. It is like a great practice: though it cultivates all virtues, it is without
Sentient beings abide in divergent views regarding the beauty or foulness of lands;
the Tathāgata abides in right wisdom.
Purity and impurity are always equal; for me, there is no fixed state.
That which should be pure is pure;
that which belongs to the category of the impure is impure.
Therefore, it is said to be "indeterminate.
That which is indeterminate regarding purity and defilement is the absence of intrinsic nature in purity and defilement.
This absence of intrinsic nature in purity and defilement is precisely the true land of equality. As for its having "no fixed direction" as its essence:
The nature of purity and impurity is empty and has no fixed location.

As for "taking the sands of the Ganges as a land," according to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, when Pūrṇa attains Buddhahood, he shall take three thousand worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to constitute a single land. Regarding "the faculties of a bodhisattva":
Some develop the faculty of faith through rejoicing in the Pure Land;
others develop the faculty of faith through wearying of the defiled land.
Though the conditions may differ in ten thousand ways, the arising of faith is one and the same.
"How could words exhaust the explanation? A straightforward mind is the pure land of a bodhisattva.
There are many kinds of straightforward minds;
furthermore, there is the straightforward mind of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
There is the straightforward mind of the two vehicles’ correct view of the Four Truths;
there is the straightforward mind of the Bodhisattva’s correct contemplation of the Middle Way;
and there is the straightforward mind that takes all Buddha-dharmas as the single suchness of the Dharma-realm.
The same applies to all subsequent categories of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). Regarding the example of "pointing at gold and calling it food": this refers to using gold to purchase food;
it serves as a metaphor for the cause being designated by the name of the effect. As for the "different names used before and after": [this refers to the shifting designations of the same entity].
The "straightforward mind" and so forth are brief at the beginning and detailed at the end;
the "Chapter on the Ten Wholesome Paths" and so forth concern causes first and effects later;
and the "perfection of patience" and so forth [concern qualities]. As for those sentient beings with right concentration:
There are three groups of sentient beings:
first, the group of those fixed in error; second, the group of those fixed in certainty;
and third, the group of those who are not fixed.
The *Abhidharmakośa* states:
"Sentient beings who commit the five deeds of immediate retribution are called the group of those fixed in the wrong (mithyātva-niyata-rāśi).
Those who have attained the Noble Path are called the group of those fixed in the right (samyaktva-niyata-rāśi)."
Other sentient beings are called the indeterminate group (*aniyata-rāśi*).
According to the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*,
bodhisattvas of the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) belong to the indeterminate group.

From the tenth stage (*bhūmi*) onward is the group of those fixed in rightness (*samyaktva-niyata-rāśi*); prior to the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) is the group of those fixed in error (*mithyātva-niyata-rāśi*).
This wisdom discerns the erroneous and the correct, and because it determines and departs [from the former], it is called "fixed in rightness. As for "dedication" (*pariṇāmana*):
For all ordinary beings who cultivate goodness, they should dedicate it toward unsurpassed bodhi.
There are three kinds of *mālā* (ornaments):
first, dedicating phenomena toward principle.
Second, the dedication of one's own merit universally to all sentient beings;
third, the dedication of causes toward the fruit. Even those in the eight difficult circumstances who hear the name of the Buddha [attain liberation].
It is like the merit of empty space.
The *Buddhanāmasūtra* states:
"Upon hearing the name of this Buddha, one who performs a single prostration..."
"All karmic obstacles and hindrances are entirely extinguished," and so forth.
According to the *Buddhāvataṃsaka-samādhi-sūtra*,
merely hearing the name of the mark of the white tuft between the Buddha's brows extinguishes the sins of birth and death accumulated over three kalpas.
The remaining characteristics are as stated in the text. As for *dhāraṇī*, it is like a jeweled pavilion and so forth.
According to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, by hearing the two characters "permanently abiding" (*nitya*), one does not fall into the evil realms.
The Devadatta Chapter. It should be understood that [the text] mentions such things as being constantly born before the Buddha through lotus-birth transformation.
There are two types of the ten wholesome actions.
First, cessation:
this refers to ceasing the ten unwholesome actions to become the ten wholesome actions.
Second, practicing the ten wholesome actions.

It consists of practicing giving, generating a spirit of generosity, performing prostrations and reverences, speaking truthful words, gentle words, harmonious words, and beneficial words; cultivating the meditation on impurity, practicing loving-kindness and compassion, and abiding in right view. As for "according to their straightforward mind": it refers to this.
This vertical clarification of the practices for the Pure Land corresponds to the thirteen stages: the straightforward mind corresponds to the ten abodes;
the practice-initiating mind corresponds to the ten practices;
and the profound mind corresponds to the ten dedications.
Subduing corresponds to the first stage;
practice corresponds to the second stage;
and dedication corresponds to the third stage.
Skillful means corresponds to the fourth stage;
maturing sentient beings corresponds to the fifth stage;
and purifying the Buddha-field corresponds to the sixth stage.
The purity of the teaching of the Dharma corresponds to the seventh stage;
the purity of wisdom corresponds to the eighth stage;
and the purity of mind corresponds to the ninth stage.
All merits are purified in correspondence with the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
The preceding seventeen lines are likewise characterized by such gradations of depth;
that is to say, as afflictions are gradually exhausted, wisdom is gradually perfected.
The mind gradually increases,
and the land gradually becomes purified.
Such is the Benevolent King.
Beginning from the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) of the Iron Wheel and ending with the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) of the fourth dhyāna,
it is said that as delusions gradually diminish, merit gradually increases; as compassion gradually deepens, the scope of transformation gradually widens.
If, as in the case of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and the manifold virtues of the Buddha-fruit, all are pure, why alone would the Buddha-field not be pure? As for Śāriputra’s reflection:
the two questions concerning cause and effect posed by Ratnakūṭa have already been answered by the Buddha.
The principle is perfect and the practice is complete;
it is only fitting that those who listen should realize and awaken to it.
That they do not awaken is because doubt remains within their hearts.
Therefore, Śāriputra relied upon the doubts of the assembly to express his mindfulness. As for "purity of things," it refers to the purity of the ponds and terraces made of the seven treasures;
since he was able to take purity as being pure, [he attained this state].
"How could one possibly discern the distinction between the impure and the non-impure?
Therefore, it is said that they are 'obscured. As for 'Spiral-Hair (Śikhin) seeing the pure,' when Śāriputra harbored doubts, the Buddha’s response resolved them."
They should also be capable of attaining awakening;
yet those who do not awaken harbor doubts and suspicions.
The World-Honored One himself said: "Who among you sees the purity of my mind in this land?"
Therefore, it is witnessed and seen by the Brahma King. That the Pure Land is like the Four Heavenly Kings and so forth is also logically consistent;
this may be inferred from the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*.
The thirty minds prior to the stages correspond to the four types of wheel-turning kings;
these are bodies born of karmic bonds that transform sentient beings,
as they have not yet attained a pure land for the purpose of transforming beings.
From the first bhūmi up to the tenth bhūmi, these are correlated with the kings of the six heavens of the desire realm and the kings of the four dhyānas.
Since one has already made vows to be born [in these realms] prior to the seventh bhūmi,
one should be born [there] from the eighth bhūmi onwards.
That is to say, because one sports with supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), purifies Buddha-fields, and transforms sentient beings, there are pure lands (*śuddhakṣetra*).
Since the ranks and differences of the royal positions of the various stages (*bhūmi*) are not the same,
it follows that the pure lands should also differ according to the ascent or descent of those stages.
This can be understood through analogy for those whose minds harbor notions of superiority and inferiority.
For while a Buddha-field ought to be pure, it appears pure;
and while it ought to be defiled, it appears defiled.
Thus one knows that the true land is fundamentally neither pure nor defiled;
this is called the Buddha’s wisdom.
Yet Śāriputra, because he perceived the pure as definitively pure, superior, and sublime, was arrogant.
Because one perceives defilement as certainly base and inferior, this is called "clinging to views" (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa);
it is not the wisdom of the Buddha. As for "attaining the patience of the non-arising of dharmas" (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti):
One realizes that defilement and purity lack intrinsic nature.
If impurity were to possess an inherent nature,
it should not be subject to transformation and subsequent disappearance.
If it were pure by nature,
it should not require pressing to manifest its purity;
the fact that it manifests purity only when pressed demonstrates that purity is not its inherent nature.
When transformed, they perish; thus, both clarity and defilement lack a fixed nature.
Therefore, because there is no arising, there is emptiness, and because there is emptiness, there is no cessation.

This may be called seeing the reality of defilement, whereby the mark of purity vanishes, one attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and enters the gate of non-duality.
Although the sutra does not explicitly state that it is neither pure nor defiled,
the principle is self-evident.
This is as in the "Life Span" chapter of the Lotus Sutra.
However, the short life of Gayā is itself made clear as long;
thus, length and brevity are not fixed.
When length and brevity are not fixed, the brief vanishes.
Although the sutra does not explicitly state that it is neither long nor short,
the principle is nonetheless self-evident; therefore,
[it is explained] in the "Chapter on the Distinction of Merits."
The bodhisattvas also realize the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, form itself is explained as emptiness,
thereby revealing that form and emptiness are not different.
The principle is evident. By this standard,
although these various Mahāyāna sūtras differ in the specific events they take as their objects,
they are one and the same in their realization of the principle and their verification of the truth.
Therefore, in the "Chapter on the Dharma-Door of Non-Duality," either arising and ceasing are both extinguished,
or sin and merit are of one single nature.
Either the mind finds nothing to grasp,
or the mouth remains silent and speaks not;
these are all different manifestations of the same practice.
It is not that there is a difference between the assembly and realization. One who knows that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are entirely impermanent—
if they awaken according to the Mahāyāna—
realizes that both the pure and the impure are merely manifestations appearing in response to beings, and possess no intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
Now, because the Hīnayāna adheres to [the reality of] substantial existence, it perceives that the transformation of phenomena is itself impermanence.

This is like Ānanda’s failure to understand that the Buddha’s body was merely a manifestation, yet he clung to the idea that it was a real illness. As for the eighty-eight *anuśayas*, these are the afflictions to be abandoned through the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
This means that these various afflictions arise from delusion regarding the Four Noble Truths. Delusion regarding the truth of suffering gives rise to the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*):
greed, hatred, ignorance, pride, doubt, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and adherence to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
Delusion regarding the truth of origin gives rise to seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*),
excluding the two views of self-identity and extremes, as well as the adherence to precepts and rituals.
Delusion regarding the truth of cessation gives rise to seven underlying tendencies in the same manner.
Eight latent dispositions (anuśaya) arise with respect to the Truth of the Path;
that is, excluding the two views of self-identity and extremes.
These constitute thirty-two [dispositions] in this Desire Realm.
In the two upper realms, there is no aversion;
for each of the Four Truths, aversion is excluded,
resulting in twenty-eight factors in each case.
When stated fully, there are eighty-eight [afflictions] within the three realms.
Regarding the ninety-eight:
this refers to the aforementioned eighty-eight of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), with ten additional afflictions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) added for abandonment.
Thus, they total ninety-eight.
As for the "ten," these refer to greed, anger, ignorance, and pride.
The desire realm possesses all four;
the form realm has three, excluding anger; and the formless realm likewise has three.
Therefore, there are ten [chapters] when the three realms are discussed together.
Regarding the "Expedient Means" chapter (*Upāya-paṛivarta*), Tiantai says:
This chapter introduces the virtues of Vimalakīrti;
it is a sūtra that Ānanda had not previously heard due to his original vow,
which the Buddha now expounds for him once again.
Therefore, at the conclusion of this chapter and the six chapters on the interior, the Buddha finished preaching the sutra and spoke again to entrust it;
thus, it was recited during the time of the Council. Regarding the elder who possesses the ten virtues:
Tiantai says: There are two types.
First, the mundane.
As explained separately,
secondly, the ten virtues of the supramundane purity are perfected as the fruit,
as stated in the sutra.
Now, let it be clarified that even hearing this sutra for a single thought-moment, or generating the mind of awakening and rejoicing in it, likewise possesses ten virtues.
First is the nobility of one's lineage;
for the bodhi of all Buddhas arises from this sutra.
They are born into the lineage of the Mother Prajñāpāramitā;
their status is high,
for at the very moment they first resolve to attain enlightenment, they have already transcended the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
A single thought of sympathetic joy surpasses the four fruits of the Two Vehicles and the three great riches.
As the *Vajra* says:
A single moment of pure faith surpasses the gift of the seven treasures three thousand times over.
Regarding the four majestic powers:
in the subsequent text, it is explained how Śakra and the Four Heavenly Kings, who had not yet had faith, develop faith, and how those who already have faith provide protection, and so forth.
Fifth is the depth of wisdom.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra states:
"One who studies the Mahāyāna possesses the Buddha-eye even though they have only the fleshly eye."
Six years old and venerable;
he has planted roots of goodness under not merely one or two Buddhas;
his seven modes of conduct are without fault.
The Great Sūtra states:
"Hearing the two characters 'eternal-abiding' prevents one from falling into the evil realms;
through the Lotus Sūtra, one is born by transformation before the Buddha."
Eighth, the eight modes of deportment are fully perfected;
seeing that all marks are non-marks is itself to see the majestic demeanor of the Buddha’s body.
Ninth, it is praised by the noble ones.
The Lotus Sūtra says:
"One should scatter heavenly flowers and give rise to the thought of regarding [the recipient] as a Buddha," and so forth.
Tenth, the inferior person returns to veneration.
The *Lotus Sūtra* says:
"There are celestial youths who serve [the Buddha], having planted various roots of goodness."
To give rise to the Mahāyāna mind is to be born into the family of the Buddhas. Regarding "patience with the non-arising of phenomena" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*),

the *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* (Renwang jing) states that it refers to the patience of subduing (*vinaya-kṣānti*) attained by the three stages of the worthy ones (*saddharmasatyaka*) prior to the [ten] stages (*bhūmi*).
In the first, second, and third stages, there is the patience of faith (*śraddhā-kṣānti*);
in the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages, the conforming patience (*anuloma-kṣānti*);
and in the seventh, eighth, and ninth stages, the patience of non-arising (*anutpāda-kṣānti*).
Regarding the "patience of cessation" (*nirodha-kṣānti*) of the Buddha-fruit at the tenth stage:
as for why it is not mentioned here as "patience of cessation," Tiantai says:
It is because of this Buddha-patience that he yields to him;
it is simply called the "patience of non-arising" (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti). As for the direction in which the mind tends:
it is like water flowing from a spring, which must inevitably tend toward the great ocean.

All who possess a mind shall surely attain the fruit of Buddhahood, for there is no water that is not water, and likewise, there is no delusion that is not enlightenment. Infinite material wealth is the foundation.
This refers to the traces manifested by one who gathers in the poor.
This is the manifestation of the trace from the fundamental source. Although he appears as a layperson, he nonetheless upholds and practices the fundamental source.
As for the term "one who observes the Vinaya":
The true nature of reality is the precept of the intrinsically pure *śīla*.
Therefore, the Chapter on Rāhula states:
"This is itself the renunciation; this is itself the full ordination."

This refers to generating the bodhicitta, departing from the house of birth-and-death to enter the house of nirvana, and receiving the precepts of the single mind that encompasses the myriad practices.
"Pure conduct" (brahmacarya) refers to abiding in the true nature of the dharmakaya, awakening to the signless pure conduct that is neither male nor female. As for "those of other paths":
Regarding the ninety-six types of dogmatic views and worldly treatises:
these are the doctrines of attachment concerning the governance of states and the management of households;
they maintain that through loyalty, one should love one's sovereign.
Filial piety consists in loving one's parents;
because each person loves their own kin, it is called the "Treatise on Love. Livelihood is one's occupation. The "four crossroads" refers to a place where roads intersect at ten directions.
This is the correct governance of the law.
Du Yu said: "It rests with the ruler to govern;
it rests with the minister to carry out affairs. *Kṣatriya*.
This refers to the "field-lord" (kṣetrapati).
The verse in the Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya states:
"At the beginning of the kalpa, they were like the gods of the Form Realm."
Later, as their craving for flavors gradually increased,
thieves arose due to the hoarding of goods;
to prevent this, they hired guards to protect the fields.
It is said that at the beginning of the kalpa, human bodies possessed radiance;
because the craving for various earth-flavors arose,
the earth-flavors ceased to appear.
Next, they ate forest dew;
greed did not arise again.
Next, they ate naturally grown non-glutinous rice.
The radiance of their bodies faded;
as their hoarding became excessive,
they subsequently divided the fields among themselves.
To prevent strife and disorder, they subsequently hired a man of virtue to serve as the lord of the fields;
this was the beginning of the Kṣatriya kings.
Furthermore, it was from this point that the clan name was changed to Gautama (newly translated as *Qiutan*).
"Gautama" is here translated as "Moon-lineage" (Candragotra) or "Sugarcane-lineage" (Ikṣvāku). The *Mahāvaipulya-mahāsannipāta-sūtra* states:
"That Great Reed King (Mahāmuñja-rāja) had no son;
he left the household life and became a seer (ṛṣi) who attained the five supernatural powers (pañcābhijñā)."
The disciple, thinking the royal seer was old, placed him in a cage and suspended it from a tree;
he then went out to gather medicinal herbs.
A hunter arrived and took the seer for a bird.
He then shot at it;
blood immediately fell to the ground and produced two sweet sprouts:
one grew into a young boy.
A daughter was born,
and her son succeeded to the royal throne; consequently,
the lineage was changed to that of the Ikṣvāku (Sugarcane) clan.
Furthermore, because he was born from being scorched by the sun, he is also called "Sun-seed" (Āditya-vaṃśa).
Later, he changed his clan name from Ikṣvāku to Śākya;
this name means "capable."
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
King Urma had four sons who were both divinely martial and intelligent.
The favored consort had a son who was stubborn,
shallow, and ugly; the consort reflected upon this.
"Although my son is advanced in years, his talent does not equal that of Kiu.
The mandate of the state's fortune must surely rest with the four younger sons.
He then devised a stratagem to cause the King to inter the four sons together.
After the four sons had departed, their followers were as numerous as clouds.
Reaching the Snowy Mountains, they built a city and established a settlement near the Kai-wei forest to the north;
the multitude was majestic in its power.
Upon hearing this, the king sighed three times and exclaimed,
"My son possesses such capability;
he shall therefore be called of the Śākya clan."
Furthermore, there are the four castes of India: Kṣatriya, Brāhmaṇa, Vaiśya, and Śūdra.
The Kṣatriyas are as described above;
the Brāhmaṇas take the study of the Way (the Veda) as their occupation.
"Vaiśya" is translated here as "sitting," meaning sitting to trade goods.
"Śūdra" refers to...
This refers to those who are farmers, officials, or scholars. "Superior wisdom" (*viśeṣa-prajñā*) is the untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) that contemplates the Four Noble Truths.
The Brahmās practice dhyāna with a mind characterized by craving and views.
If one lacks right wisdom, one cannot escape saṃsāra. The World Protectors are the Four Heavenly Kings.
The one of the east is Dhṛtarāṣṭra, which means "Lord of the Realm."
In the south is Virūḍhaka,
which is translated here as "Lord of Increase.
In the west is Virūpākṣa.
Furthermore, he is called "Mixed Speech" (Kubera) and also "Lord of the Ugly Eyes.
He is Vaiśravaṇa of the northern quarter.
"This one known as the Lord of Much Learning—this body is impermanent.
There are two kinds of impermanence: first, the impermanence of phenomena (*dharma*).

This refers to the impermanence of things as they undergo transformation through the passage of the four seasons, such as the aging of one's physical appearance; this is the impermanence of phenomena.
Second is the impermanence of principle.
This means that conditioned phenomena, by their very nature, undergo transformation and change from moment to moment;
how could they wait for the falling of leaves or the appearance of white hair before becoming impermanent?
The contemplation of suffering regarding the lower realms is likewise.
If the arising of illness in the formless realm constitutes suffering,
this matter is indeed suffering.

If one knows that the five aggregates (pañca-skandha), being of the nature of outflows (sāsrava) and conditioned (saṃskṛta), are fundamentally suffering, this is the suffering of principle (tattva-duḥkha).
The third, the contemplation of emptiness (śūnyatā-vipaśyanā), also has two aspects:
if one regards the dissolution of the body and the destruction of form as emptiness, [this is the first].
This is the fact:
if one practices, the five aggregates (skandhas) are conditioned by nature, lacking solidity, and being momentarily impermanent, their essence returns to emptiness.
This is the principle.

Furthermore, this is the emptiness of impermanence based on the causes and conditions of the "half-syllables" (semi-literal teachings), and it is not the emptiness of dependent origination based on the "full-syllables" (complete teachings).
To contemplate this principle of suffering is called the contemplation of the truth of suffering and so forth. As for suffering:
The three types of suffering: the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), which is the nature of painful feeling (*duḥkhavedanā*).
Second is the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkha*), which is the nature of pleasant feeling (*sukhavedanā*). Third is the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāraduḥkha*).
It is the nature of neutral feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*).
The desire realm possesses all three types of suffering;
the form realm possesses the latter two.
In the formless realm, there is only the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*). Furthermore, there are eight types of suffering as previously explained. As for the ten similes:

The five metaphors of a mass of foam, a bubble, a plantain tree, a floating cloud, and lightning pertain to the Small Vehicle’s (Hīnayāna) teaching on emptiness as impermanence through the "half-letters" (*ardha-akṣara*).

The five metaphors of a mirage, an illusion, a dream, an echo, and a reflection pertain to the Great Vehicle’s (Mahāyāna) teaching on the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva-śūnyatā*) through the "full-letters" (*pūrṇa-akṣara*). Regarding "non-arising is like the earth": the four great elements constitute the body.
The skin, flesh, tendons, and bones constitute earth;
the blood, marrow, eyes, and tears constitute water;
the movements, turns, and breaths constitute wind.
Pervasive bodily warmth constitutes fire.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharmakośa* states that its nature is solidity.
Moisture is the nature of water;
warmth is the nature of fire;
movement is the nature of wind.
Furthermore, to grasp the earth element as the self is the mark of a sentient being; to grasp the fire element as the self is likewise [the mark of a sentient being].
This is precisely the mark of self.
The nature of fire is to blaze upward, which shares the same characteristic as the conceit of "I-am-ness" (asmimāna).
One clings to the water element as being the self.
This is precisely the mark of personhood.
Human affairs change with the times, just as water conforms to its vessel;
they are likewise identical in nature.
To grasp at the wind-element as a self is the mark of a "living being" (jīvaka).
The uninterrupted continuity of the cessation of that wind is called "life-span."
Therefore, the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra says:
"That which emits the out-breath is called life-span.
Thus, the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra states:
If the mind grasps at signs, it immediately clings to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.
If one grasps at even a single mark of a self, that is to simultaneously cling to all four great elements. To be without knowledge is to be like grass and wood.
Grasses and trees lack sentience;
they flourish and fall depending on the four seasonal elements.
The conscious mind is likewise.
Assuming different objects, there is sorrow and grief;
having relied upon conditions, there is discrimination.
Thus, in its very self-nature, it is devoid of cognition. As for the thirty-six constituents:

The twelve external characteristics are hair, body hair, nails, teeth, tears, sweat, saliva, mucus, feces, urine, filth, and impurities. The twelve components of the physical vessel are as follows: [list omitted].
The skin, flesh, blood, sinews, bones, marrow, fat, grease, brain, and membranes—these constitute the twelve internal components.

Furthermore, there are the liver, gallbladder, intestines, stomach, spleen, kidneys, heart, and lungs; the solid organs (*sōng-zàng*) and hollow organs (*shú-zàng*); and the red, white, and pale fluids. Such is the marvel of form.
This means that those of the Two Vehicles do not know that the five aggregates are all empty and constitute the Buddha-body;
instead, they take the thirty-two marks as the Buddha-body.
Consequently, they suffer the afflictions of the golden thorns and the horse-barley.
How could one grow weary of that and rejoice in this?
This is intended to demonstrate that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of the Mahāyāna are fundamentally empty;
birth in the royal palace is itself non-birth.
Whether extinguished at the twin trees or not, the six-foot form is itself the true Buddha-body;
thus it is said that the Buddha-body is the Dharma-body. As for "transcending the three realms":
This means awakening to the fact that the three realms are like an illusion.
"Not subsumed within the aggregates" means that the aggregates and sense bases are themselves empty.
"The eight extremes" refers to the eight directions. "To apply thought" means to direct, to cast, or to place. "The six supernormal powers" refers to...
First is the supernormal power of the realm of psychic transformation,
which refers to manifesting either a large body or a small body.
Second is the divine ear.
Hearing sounds beyond obstructions;
third, the divine eye,
which sees things beyond obstructions.
Fourth is the knowledge of others' minds,
because it knows others.
Fifth is the recollection of past lives.

Because of knowing past lives; because of the exhaustion of the six outflows, meaning all afflictions have been extinguished. Regarding the three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*): [the first is] knowing past lives... [the second is] the destruction of the outflows... [the third is] the knowledge of the non-arising of future suffering]. Because all afflictions have been exhausted, there are the three types of clear knowledge.
First is the clarity of recollecting past lives, through which one knows former existences;
second is the clarity of the divine eye.
Third is the clear knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*). To know phenomena in a superficial manner is called supernormal power (*abhijñā*);
to profoundly examine causes and conditions is called clear knowledge (*vidyā*).
Furthermore, the *Abhidharmakośa* states:
"The clear knowledge of past lives eliminates delusion regarding the past;
the divine eye eliminates delusion regarding the future."
The exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya) eliminates ignorance regarding the three periods of time; the other three do not do so.
Therefore, they are called "penetrations" (abhiñjñā) but are not called "clear knowledges" (vidyā).
*Annotated Explanation of the Vimalakīrti Sūtra from Guanzhong*, Scroll One;
*Excerpts from the Annotated Explanation of the Vimalakīrti Sūtra from Guanzhong*, Scroll Two, composed by the Śramaṇa Dao... [name obscured].
In the "Chapter on Disciples," Vinaya Master Xuán states:

Because their training follows that of the precepts, they are called "those who do not understand. As for the Bodhisattvas who convert others externally, they do not remain constantly by the Buddha's side; because they come only briefly to receive the five precepts and do not serve him constantly, they are ranked [below]. This applies to the Śrāvakas and not to the other two vehicles.
Tiantai says: There are five intentions for the arrival of this chapter.

First, in order to manifest the virtues of Vimalakīrti, [the text] describes how the great disciples were unable to respond to his inquiries, thereby fully revealing the excellence of Vimalakīrti’s merit.
Faith gives rise to the mind.
Mañjuśrī enters [the state of] ... and through two methods causes those śrāvakas who have not yet entered the stage of certainty (*samyaktvaniyāma*) to turn their minds toward the Great Vehicle.
If they are unable to endure this, they immediately abandon the Small Vehicle and return to the Great.
This constitutes the third stage of the practice for attaining the Pure Land.
If one hears that the provisional and ultimate [teachings] of the Bodhisattvas are inconceivable,
one will gradually come to recognize the two lands of the Buddhas— the True and the Responsive.
Fourth, for the śrāvakas who have already entered the stage of certainty, they become like clarified butter;
yet when taught the Śrāvaka [vehicle], it is as if they were previously deaf to the *Avataṃsaka*,
and ordinary beings do not change their countenance.
Therefore, for those of the two vehicles who progress gradually, it is like milk;
subsequently hearing the Āgamas and attaining the four fruits is like curd.
He was told that the fruits of his pure name and equalizing wisdom were not yet true,
like raw butter. Next,
he heard of Prajñā, who permitted him to transmit the Mahāyāna but had not yet granted him a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
Therefore, it is like matured ghee (*sarpis*);
later, the preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Nirvāṇa* sūtras, which all lead back to the Buddha Vehicle as the "cream of cream" (*sarpirmaṇḍa*),
refers to these five flavors of teaching as being progressively presented in relation to the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
They are not Bodhisattvas. To provide a seal of authentication for the established scriptures,
it is said that what was previously taught was all not spoken in the presence of the Buddha.
Now, having presented this before the Buddha,
that which is ratified by the Tathāgata becomes a sūtra.
The commentary states:
"His mind suspended, he penetrates through silence" means that the Sage’s mind illuminates the preceding mind from a distance,
penetrating its vision in silent stillness.
What need is there for words?

As for "the hidden mechanism responding in obscurity," it means that because one perceives the mechanism in profound stillness and responds in secret accord, they thus come together. "Not within the three realms" means...
Śāriputra enters the eight dhyānas of the Hīnayāna as well as the samādhi of cessation;
these are all attained by means of the body and mind within the three realms.
The Bodhisattva, however, abides in the samādhi of true reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa).
That is, the true wisdom of the Dharmakāya realizes that which is not a dharma of the triple world.
As the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra says:
"The bhikṣu, detached from all desires and from evil, unwholesome dharmas..."
By relying on the concentration of the stage of access (anāgamya), one attains the first dhyāna,
which possesses vitarka and vicāra,
as well as joy, bliss, and one-pointedness of mind.
Because they are free from the fire of desire, these are called vitarka and vicāra.
Furthermore, he reflects:
"Vitarka and vicāra disturb the meditative mind."
Like waves upon water,
like calling out in sleep— thus,
in various ways, one censures and awakens from applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*).
With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, there is internal clarity;
with the mind focused on a single point, free from applied and sustained thought,
there is the joy and happiness born of concentration.
He enters the second dhyāna.
Furthermore, he contemplates the many faults of joy;
having attained the state where joy is absent and sorrow is transcended, he dwells free from joy.
Abandoning directed thought and evaluation, with mindfulness and clear comprehension, he experiences bodily pleasure; he enters the third dhyāna.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the faults of pleasure as he did those of joy.
Seeking the state where the mind is unmoving, neither painful nor pleasant,
one enters the fourth dhyāna, purified by equanimity and mindfulness.
Furthermore, one contemplates that form has many faults;
one contemplates the emptiness within the body,
and external forms are likewise so.
One attains the sphere of infinite space.
Furthermore, as the practitioner contemplates that space is infinite,
consciousness takes many objects and becomes highly distracted.
Therefore, abandoning the object of space and taking consciousness alone as the object is called the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).
Furthermore, this consciousness is infinite; if it were excessive, it would become distracted.
Therefore, one censures consciousness and praises the contemplation of the sphere of nothingness.
In this state, the four aggregates are a source of affliction;
non-perception is like an abscess, and perception is like a disease.

Entering the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the attainment of non-perception, the attainment of cessation, and the heaven of non-perception is called "having remaining characteristics"; since these formless states are all composed of the four aggregates, one enters the attainment of cessation by extinguishing sensation, perception, and other mental activities.

Therefore, these are all the body and mind of the three realms. Now, the Bodhisattva, through the correct contemplation of the Middle Way, perceives that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of the three realms are neither born nor extinguished; this is definitively established as the true *nirodha-samāpatti* (the meditative attainment of cessation). As for "the spirit perishing along with [the body]": [The text continues: ...it is said that when the body perishes, the spirit also perishes. This is because the spirit is dependent upon the body. Just as when one dies, the spirit departs from the body, so too, when the body perishes, the spirit likewise perishes. Furthermore, it is said that the spirit is subtle and the body is coarse. Because the coarse perishes first, the subtle necessarily follows. Moreover, the spirit is impermanent and the body is also impermanent. Since both are impermanent, they perish together. Furthermore, the spirit is produced by the body and the body is produced by the spirit. Since they arise simultaneously, they perish simultaneously. Also, the spirit is the master and the body is the servant. When the master perishes, the servant necessarily perishes. For these reasons, it is said that when the body perishes, the spirit also perishes. However, this is not the case. Why? Because the spirit is eternal and the body is impermanent. Since the eternal does not perish, how could it perish along with the impermanent? Furthermore, the spirit is unconditioned and the body is conditioned. Since the unconditioned does not perish, how could it perish along with the conditioned? Moreover, the spirit is the cause and the body is the effect. Since the cause does not perish, how could the effect perish along with it? Also, the spirit is the root and the body is the branch. Since the root does not perish, how could the branch perish along with it? For these reasons, it is known that the spirit does not perish along with the body. It is only because sentient beings do not understand the principle of the spirit’s eternity that they mistakenly claim the spirit perishes along with the body. Thus, the Buddha taught that the spirit is eternal. If the spirit were impermanent, there would be no continuity of rebirth. Because the spirit is eternal, there is continuity of rebirth. Therefore, it is known that the spirit is eternal and does not perish along with the body. Furthermore, the spirit is the knower and the body is the known. Since the knower does not perish, how could the known perish along with it? Also, the spirit is the subject and the body is the object. Since the subject does not perish, how could the object perish along with it? For these reasons, it is known that the spirit does not perish along with the body. Since the thinker does not perish, how could the thought perish along with it? Also, the spirit is the feeler and the body is the felt. Since the feeler does not perish, how could the felt perish along with it? For these reasons, it is known that the spirit does not perish along with the body. Since the agent does not perish, how could the instrument perish along with it? Also, the spirit is the experiencer and the body is the experienced. Since the experiencer does not perish, how could the experienced perish along with it? For these reasons, it is known that the spirit does not perish along with the body. Therefore, it is known that the spirit is eternal and does not perish along with the body. Furthermore, the spirit is the refuge and the body is the refuged. Since the refuge does not perish, how could the refuged perish along with it? Also, the spirit is the support and the body is the supported. Since the support does not perish, how could the supported perish along with it? For these reasons, it is known that the spirit does not perish along with the body. Since the seed does not perish, how could the fruit perish along with it? Also, the spirit is the source and the body is the derivative. Since the source does not perish, how could the derivative perish along with it? For these reasons, it is known that the spirit does not perish along with the body. It is only because sentient beings do not understand the principle of the spirit’s eternity that they mistakenly claim the spirit perishes along with the body. Thus, the Buddha taught that the spirit is eternal. If the spirit were impermanent, there would be no continuity of rebirth. Because the spirit is eternal, there is continuity of rebirth. Therefore, it is known that the spirit is eternal and does not perish along with the body. Furthermore, the spirit is the light and the body is the darkness. Since the light does not perish, how could the darkness perish along with it? Also, the spirit is the clarity and the body is the turbidity. Since the clarity does not perish, how could the turbidity perish along with it? For these reasons, it is known that the spirit does not perish along with the body. It is only because sentient beings do not understand the principle of the spirit’s eternity that they mistakenly claim the spirit perishes along with the body. Thus, the Buddha taught that the spirit is eternal. If the spirit were impermanent, there would be no continuity of rebirth. Because the spirit is eternal, there is continuity of rebirth. Therefore, it is known that the spirit is eternal and does not perish along with the body. Furthermore, the spirit is the constant and the body is the transient.
That is to say, bodhi cannot be attained by means of the body, nor can it be attained by means of the mind.
The body is itself formless and without distinction;
the mind is itself rootless and without abiding.
Because it is neither born nor extinguished, it is called "true extinction.
Such is the extinction-samādhi of the Mahāsattva.

As for the "Dharma of the Path," it is the very emptiness of the aggregates (*skandha*). "Manifesting the affairs of ordinary beings" refers to skillful means engaging with the provisional. "The mind does not dwell within or without" means:
The emptiness of the nature of the three locations is the actual cessation of the mind;
therefore, it does not abide. Regarding "unmoving amidst all views":
clinging to names is what constitutes a view.
The two extremes are called "movement.
In the four foundations of mindfulness of the Two Vehicles, one contemplates the body as impure to destroy the inversion of purity,
and contemplates sensation as suffering to destroy the inversion of pleasure.
Contemplating the impermanence of the mind breaks the inversion of permanence;
contemplating the selflessness of phenomena breaks the inversion of self.
Other chapters follow this same pattern.
This is called the practice of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment by those of the two vehicles who are moved by various views.
As for the four foundations of mindfulness in the Mahāyāna,
one contemplates that the nature of the body is empty, being neither pure nor impure.
One contemplates that feeling does not exist internally, externally, or in between, and is neither suffering nor pleasure.
One contemplates that the mind exists only as a provisional name, being neither permanent nor impermanent.
One contemplates that phenomena are like illusions and transformations, being neither self nor non-self.
The other chapters follow this same pattern.
This is called the Mahāyāna, which is unshakable by any views and cultivates the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
It is explained in detail in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Sarvadharma-apracāra-vidyā*.
Regarding "not severing the afflictions":
because the nature of the afflictions is empty, they are said not to be severed.
The clinging to the dharmas of the Two Vehicles as being substantially real is like [clinging to] the afflictions as being substantially real.
Therefore, one enters by means of severance.
Because the Bodhisattva realizes that the nature of afflictions is empty, he enters without severing them. As for the seven messengers:
Greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and doubt constitute the five [afflictions];
the view of a self-identity and the view of extremes constitute the sixth view;
and the clinging to precepts and rituals and the clinging to views constitute the seventh grasping-affliction (*parāmarśa*).
The nine fetters (saṃyojana) are as previously described. As for my remaining silent at that time, O World-Honored One, one should have called out, "World-Honored One, I remained silent at that time.
It was only because the expression was concise in the Sanskrit language. "Maudgalyāyana-parivarta" is the Sanskrit pronunciation.
The *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra* translates [the term] as "pea" (*húdòu*).
The *Dharmaskandha-pāda-śāstra* refers to it as "Maudgalyāyanaputra," which here means "mung bean" (*lǜdòuzi*).
The new commentary says: "It is like gathering beans.
Furthermore, previously, Śāriputra, who was foremost in wisdom, rebuked Maudgalyāyana on account of his meditative concentration.
The foremost in meditative concentration is reprimanded by means of the teaching on the Dharma.
The reason these two [foremost disciples] are reprimanded in an alternating manner is that concentration and wisdom are the gateway to all practices.
Therefore, it cannot be fixed unilaterally.

That which is fixed as profound must be characterized by wisdom and clarity; that which is characterized by wisdom and clarity must be fixed as profound. Regarding the statement that "dharmas have no self and so forth": [this refers to the absence of a permanent, unitary, independent self within all phenomena].
In the Hīnayāna, one contemplates the refutation of the self to realize non-self,
realizing only the first fruit [of the path] and so forth.
Now, in the Mahāyāna, the reality-mark (dharmatā) is the non-duality of self and non-self.
Since even a self cannot be apprehended,
how could that which is not-self be apprehended?
This is the true meaning of non-self, the reality-nature and ultimate characteristic of all phenomena.
By realizing this selflessness, one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
How could the Bodhisattvas of the seventh stage be the same as those of the Lesser Vehicle? As for those who have departed from birth and death:
if there were birth in the prior limit and death in the subsequent limit, [they would not be liberated].
Therefore, the intermediate state is called "life-span.
Now, the Bodhisattva abides in the true reality (*dharmakāya-tathatā*);
because it is unarisen, there is no prior limit (*pūrvakoṭi*).
Because it is not extinguished, there is no subsequent [existence].
Because there is no prior or subsequent, the nature of the life-span is empty. Regarding "the extinction of all marks":
the Hīnayāna teaches that dharmas possess the four marks of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing, and that these marks undergo transition.
Now, the nature of reality (dharmatā) in the Mahāyāna is inherently quiescent and free from the four marks. Regarding "being free from vitarka and vicāra":
when one grasps at marks and gives rise to the mind, one speaks of the existence of vitarka and vicāra;
because it is free from such marks and is a mere provisional designation, there is no vitarka or vicāra. As for "the myriad dharmas and myriad conditions": [they are...]
Because all phenomena lack fixed nature, there are no phenomena.
Because conditions lack fixed conditions, there are no conditions.
For example, the body is the realm of bodhi; when it is fully realized as the multitude [of dharmas], it is the absence of phenomena.
Just as an infant, a youth, an adult, and an elder take on various forms through a multitude of conditions, so too form has no fixed form. As for the statement that "dharmas do not belong to causes":
false dharmas possess arising and ceasing, and therefore they do belong to causes and conditions.
Because that true Dharma which arises neither arises nor ceases, it does not belong to causes and conditions.
As for "being unmoved by any extremes," because it is free from the four propositions, it is unmoved by any extremes.
For one who has departed from contemplative practice, false consciousness arises by taking marks as its object; thus it is called "contemplation.
True wisdom, however, illuminates the absence of marks.
Because it is signless, there is no contemplation.
Furthermore, because the mind that grasps signs conditions the arising of signs, it is called "activity.
The mind free from signs is without arising.
Because there is no arising, there is no activity. Kāśyapa, this term "tortoise" is used to signify clarity;
it refers to one who knows the three periods of time.
Some say it means "Drinking Light" (Kāśyapa),
which also signifies "illumination.
This refers to the censure of dhūta practices.
In the Hīnayāna, one shakes off and remains unstained by and unattached to four matters;
having few desires and being contented is called *dhūta*.
Now, in the great matter of the Pure Name (*Vimalakīrti*), regarding the three realms, the five aggregates, bodhi, and nirvāṇa, it is as in the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
To shake off [defilements] while being without grasping and without dwelling is called *dhūta*.
Therefore, the *Lotus Sūtra* says:
"This sūtra is difficult to uphold."
If one is able to maintain this, they are called one who maintains the precepts and practices *dhūta*.
Furthermore, the *Suvikrāntavikramī-paripṛcchā-sūtra* (The Sutra of the Son of Heaven of Good Abiding Mind) states:
"*Dhūta* means to shake off."
I say that such a person is able to thoroughly shake off greed, anger, and delusion within the three realms and the six sense bases.
Thus shaken off, they neither grasp nor reject, neither cultivate nor cling.
I say that this person is well-versed in dhūta.
"Dhūta" is translated here as "shaking off.
Furthermore, within the practice of dhūta, there are two types.
First, according to the seasons,
as in the Brahmajāla Sūtra,
the spring and autumn months constitute the two-month period for travel.
The mind is like the extreme cold of winter and the extreme heat of summer; therefore, one observes the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat).
During spring and autumn, when the weather is temperate, one may travel accordingly.
Second, regarding traveling accordingly:
There are twelve. The *Sifen lü* (Dharmaguptaka-vinaya) states:
first, the three robes alone.
Second, wearing rag-robes;
third, always begging for food;
fourth, not performing the ritual of leaving food remaining.
5. Sitting in one place;
6. Eating in one sitting;
7. A forest (araṇya), here meaning a soundless place; 8. Among tombs.
9. Under a tree;
10. sitting in the open air;
11. following the seat.
Regarding the twelve who always sit but cannot be universal:
among the various voices of Kāśyapa, there are two practices that are superior.

First, because he does not yet possess the bodhisattva’s objectless great compassion, he is not universal; whereas [the others], by virtue of that objectless great compassion, are able to be universal.
Next, he specifically rebukes him, saying:
"One who dwells in the dharma of equanimity should proceed next to beg for alms.
Thus he rebukes the śrāvaka practitioner of dhūta asceticism.
Begging for food is merely for the sake of sustaining the five aggregates with few desires;
it is not the same as the Bodhisattva’s practice of sustaining the Dharma-body through firm abiding in right contemplation.
The Dharma-body, moreover, does not eat.
The body possesses harmony;
the Dharma-body does not receive a body within the three realms. As for the characteristic of an empty village, there are two kinds of villages.
First is the external aggregate,
which is the village or town;
second is the internal aggregate.
These are the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*). Therefore, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* states that the "village of the six sense faculties" is where bandits dwell.
This means that if there are people, goods, men, or women within the various external aggregates, they become objects of observation.
If an empty village has no people and contains only bandits, tigers, wolves, corpses, and venomous snakes, it cannot be a place of delight.
If the six sense faculties of a bodhisattva are like those described in the Lotus Sūtra, [it is likewise].
The eight hundred merits and the one thousand two hundred merits are like the people and things found in a village.
Now, the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*) of ordinary beings are empty and devoid of merit;
they possess only the three poisonous snakes of sensation (*vedanā*), the bandits of false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), and the corpses of deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*).

Therefore, it is not to be delighted in. As for "not abandoning the eight wrongs": if one abandons the eight wrongs and enters the eight liberations, this is the food of the meditative joy of the Hīnayāna.
If, however, one enters the eight liberations without abandoning the eight wrongs—
Taking the joy of meditation as food for the Mahāyāna;
if one abandons the eightfold wrong path and enters the eightfold right path,
taking the joy of the Dharma as food for the Hīnayāna.
If one does not abandon false appearances and enters the True Dharma, taking the joy of the Mahāyāna as food, then from now on this is called "Manifesting the Joy of the Mahāyāna.

This explains that the meditative delight (*dhyānāsvāda*) of the Mahāyāna supersedes the two types of food of the Hīnayāna, O Kāśyapa. Regarding the phrase "not having afflictions, etc.": [it means that] they do not possess afflictions and so forth.
Because the nature of the Mahāyāna’s food of joy in the equality of the Dharma is inherently pure, it is neither existent nor non-existent.
Because the mind-nature is the food of dhyāna-joy in the tranquility and equality of cessation, concentration is neither entering nor exiting.
Because saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are equal, he dwells in neither; thus, he does not consume the offerings of others in vain.
In the Hīnayāna, consuming the food [of others] constitutes a violation of the four grave offenses (pārājika).
They are not diligent in the three types of action:
those of superior faculties do not practice seated meditation;
those of middling faculties do not engage in recitation.
Those of inferior faculties do not manage monastic affairs;
they eat as those who are in debt.
Those who have attained the first fruit eat with those of like mind.
An Arhat eats for himself because he is one who is worthy of offerings; likewise,
if one in the Mahāyāna does not generate the bodhicitta and abide in the contemplation of equality, [he too acts for his own sake].
They are not true renunciants;
therefore, they are all said to be "empty consumers" of the faithful offerings of others. Subhūti is called Shanji (Worthy of Goodness), and is also called Kongsheng (Empty Birth).
He was also called Subhūti because,
at the time of his birth, all the rooms of the house became empty;
his parents, deeming this inauspicious, were about to consult a physiognomist.
The physiognomist’s divination stated:
"Greatly auspicious and most excellent.
Therefore, he was named Sudarśana.
Some say: Subhūti is named "Good Appearance" because wholesome signs appear within him.
However, this is primarily intended to manifest his emptiness, as he is foremost in the realization of emptiness.
For example, Rāhula’s six-year stay in the womb signifies that his secret conduct (*guhyacaryā*) was foremost;
Kāśyapa’s golden complexion signifies that he was adorned by the purity of his dhūta practices;
and Kālodāyin—translated here as "Black Radiance"—[signifies...]
Upāli was foremost among those who established the rules for defiled and pure conduct.
Furthermore, Subhūti was foremost among the disciples in understanding emptiness and being free from contention.
In the Hīnayāna, entering the fourth dhyāna and contemplating the conditions of sentient beings such that one does not contend with things is called "non-contention" (araṇā).
Yet, by abandoning existence and realizing emptiness, or by discarding saṃsāra and grasping at nirvāṇa, they have not yet escaped this contention.
Now, the Mahāyāna practitioner of Vimalakīrti abides in the contemplation of the Middle Way:
it is neither defiled nor pure, neither arising nor ceasing;
self and non-self are non-dual in their essential nature.
The fundamental nature of birth-and-death and nirvana is equal;
this is called the true absence of contention.
Therefore, he was rebuked.

Furthermore, because those of the Hīnayāna take the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) as their object when entering meditative contemplation, they perceive emptiness; yet when emerging from contemplation, they take the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) as their object, and thus perceive existence.
In this way, to abandon existence and grasp at emptiness is not the true understanding of emptiness.
Now, in the Mahāyāna of Vimalakīrti, form is not different from emptiness, and emptiness is not different from form.
It is neither existent nor non-existent, neither grasped nor abandoned.
One penetrates the characteristics of all phenomena without obstruction.
I prostrate to the one who is like space, having no dependence;
he is truly named the foremost in understanding emptiness.
Thus was he rebuked.
Question:
What is the *araṇā-samādhi* (concentration of non-contention) of the Hīnayāna? Answer:
The *Abhidharmakośakārikā* states: "The absence of contention (*araṇā*) is conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
It belongs to the final dhyāna, is immovable, and pertains to the three continents regarding that which has not yet arisen."
The defilements with objective referents in the desire realm consist of the eight mundane knowledges among the ten knowledges;
one dwells in meditative concentration within the fourth dhyāna.
Among the six types of arhats, those of immovable nature do not take the northern continent as an object within the four continents,
because they lack the notion of "mine."
It takes only the future as its object,
because the past and present have already ceased.
Within the three realms, it takes only the desire realm as its object.
Because they possess afflictions and delusions.
Furthermore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:
"Among the ten disciples, they secretly practice the conduct of Bodhisattvas while outwardly manifesting as Śrāvakas."
This means that before the Tathāgata appeared in the world, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana manifested as followers of external paths;
Uruvilvākāśyapa manifested as a fire-worshipper;
and Mahākāśyapa manifested as a pure-practicing Brahmin.
Rāhula and Aniruddha manifested themselves in royal palaces to experience the five sensual pleasures;
Śāriputra manifested as one of keen wisdom;
Cūḍapanthaka manifested as one who was dull-witted; and Maudgalyāyana manifested as one of noble status.
Upāli manifested as one of low station;
Pūrṇa manifested as one of vast learning;
Kātyāyana manifested as one skilled in debate.
When the Tathāgata attained enlightenment, he immediately led those of similar capacity to realize the fruit of a śrāvaka.
Now, in order to lead those of the Lesser Vehicle into the Great Vehicle, he inquired after their illnesses;
each declined, saying they were unable to go.
This causes those to be transformed to abandon the Lesser Vehicle and return to the Great Vehicle;
it serves as a skillful means for gradually bestowing the prediction of enlightenment according to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Regarding the filling of the bowl to the brim, some say it refers to Śubhavyūha.

Because he maintains the understanding of emptiness, he goes to Vimalakīrti to manifest the characteristics of wondrous existence through refutation; thus he is shown [here]. As for "not destroying the body":
because the śrāvakas regard the body as suffering, they extinguish the body to return to quiescence.

The "one mark" is the mark of quiescence (*śānta-lakṣaṇa*). When a bodhisattva contemplates the body as arising from conditions and lacking intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the body is naturally and fundamentally quiescent even without waiting for its destruction. As for the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*):
Killing one's father, killing one's mother, killing an arhat, shedding the blood of a Buddha, and causing a schism in the Saṃgha that breaks the Wheel of Dharma:
the first two violate kindness,
while the latter three betray virtue.
Therefore, it is called "rebellion.
Among the severities of karmic bondage, nothing exceeds this;
