there is no bondage that is not false.

"Because all delusions are fundamentally true, even the bonds of transgression are the very mark of liberation; the nature of false views and the other shore are no different"—these three phrases constitute the essential meaning of the Guanzhong [Commentary].
One may accept food because it is characterized by equality—being neither deviant nor correct, neither difficult nor vexing, and neither pure nor impure.
This is the intention of Tiantai:

he rebukes Subhūti for his two-vehicle attachment to partial emptiness as a "deviant view," and for his failure to abide in the Middle Way or the further shore, characterizing him as one who has merely reached the illusory city.
It is not that there are no difficulties.
When one is defiled by attachment to nirvana and alienated from the purity of the *dharmatā*, one encounters the eight difficulties of the "transformed city.
What are their characteristics?
Answer: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"It would be better to let sentient beings fall into the hells of the three miserable realms."
He does not cause sentient beings to enter the paths of the two vehicles;
rather, he regards the paths of seeing, cultivation,
and no-more-learning of the Hīnayāna as a hardship within the three evil realms.
Permanently adhering to non-self is a difficulty for this continent.
Emerging from contemplation to take the mundane as an object, and entering contemplation to take the ultimate truth as an object,
constitutes the difficulty of being before or after the Buddha.
Not seeing the Dharma-body and not hearing the Middle Way,
they are born deaf and blind;
though they discourse on arising and ceasing, they do not understand non-arising.
To be possessed of worldly wisdom and eloquence,
yet to sink into emptiness and linger in quiescence,
is difficult even for the long-lived devas.
The Great Sūtra states, "ten thousand kalpas," and so forth;
this is because it is the root for generating the Great [Vehicle].
For this reason, it constitutes a difficult obstacle to true nirvāṇa.
There are those who exceed the afflictions of ordinary beings and the eight difficulties;
how can one not stand in awe?
Regarding the absence of pure fields of merit and the falling into slanderous speech, there are two differing views.
From this analogy it can be seen that "equal and without difference" means that in the Guanzhong tradition,
equality and the single nature are taken as being without difference; whereas in the Tiantai tradition,
ordinary beings are said to be stuck in duality and the Two Vehicles are said to be stuck in emptiness.
Although their stagnations differ, they are equal in obstructing the Middle Way and are no different from one another. Regarding "setting down the bowl and wishing to depart," Tiantai says:
Subhūti was subjected to persecution;
he suddenly heard [the Buddha] falsely praise him for his understanding of emptiness, yet he too lost [his way].
Therefore, Vimalakīrti responds by establishing [the teaching] through illusion and transformation. Previously, Maudgalyāyana rebuked Pūrṇa for his improper salutation while preaching the Dharma;
this chapter rebukes the affliction of faulty faculties.
Some say that the phrase "observing the human mind" is the world-accommodating teaching (*loka-anuvartana-siddhānta*),
while the phrase "the fundamental source" is the remedial teaching (*pratipakṣa-siddhānta*).
The practice of the Great Way is the first principle of the *siddhānta*. Therefore,
regarding the question of the *siddhānta* for those of Mahāyāna capacity,
this teaching is named after its appearance in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*.
In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the Sanskrit term *siddhānta* is translated here as "establishment of the tenet" (*zōngchéng*),
and it is also called "conclusion" (*mò*).
It is like the Seal of the True Aspect (yathābhūtalakṣaṇamudrā) and its kind.
That seal seals the principle;
this ink preserves the fixed teaching.
This consists of four kinds.
First is the world-siddhānta (worldly standpoint).
It is for the sake of sentient beings who have developed roots of goodness, so that by relying on worldly names and signs, they may give rise to the desire for the present life and develop faith.
Second is the *puruṣapudgalasiddhānta* (the standpoint for individuals),
which is established so that those who have already planted roots of goodness may cause them to increase according to their respective faculties and conditions.
Third is the *pratipakṣasiddhānta* (the standpoint of remediation).

The fourth is the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (ultimate standpoint), established for the sake of sentient beings who, although they have planted roots of goodness, have not yet attained accomplishment because their [roots] are obstructed by heavy afflictions;
it is taught as a means to provide an antidote.
It is also spoken to encompass the principle for those sentient beings who have long practiced cultivation.
These, then, are the first three which accord with the faculties;
the fourth subsumes the underlying principle.
Regarding the first three, there are again two types: those who have not yet attained faith are caused to give rise to faith.
Once the world has gained faith, it causes them to initiate practice;
this is established as the antidote for human beings.
Furthermore, there are two ways of initiating practice.
The arising of wholesome conduct establishes the person;
the arising of the abandonment of unwholesome conduct establishes the remedy.

For these reasons, within the signless Dharma, the Tathāgata—in accordance with principle and in conformity with the faculties of beings—generates faith, gives rise to practice, produces the wholesome, and eliminates the unwholesome, thereby flowing forth eighty-four thousand teachings.
Because the various distinctions among other teaching gates all lead toward Great Bodhi; Kātyāyana— here translated as "Gāngshèng" (Rigid Remainder)—
some say means "ornamentation," while the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* calls him "Tishafǎzhǒng" (Shaving-Hair-Caste).

The reason for this is not yet clear. To speak of the dharma of the true mark (*dharmatā*) in terms of the mental activities of arising and ceasing refers to what is called arising and ceasing as the phenomena produced through conditions (*pratītyasamutpanna-dharma*), which are subject to transformation by the four marks.
Phenomena that arise and cease are born from causes and conditions.
The essence of dependently originated phenomena is what is called the true nature (dharmatā) which lacks intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva).
Furthermore, because the Hīnayāna arises from grasping, it possesses the four meanings of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
Because one grasps that cessation has the meaning of quiescence,
the first four are characterized by aversion,
while the last one is characterized by aspiration.
Now, because the Mahāyāna realizes that which is neither born nor extinguished, it is the meaning of the true mark (*dharmatā*).
Yet, when Kātyāyanīputra speaks of dependent origination as impermanent, he is employing the teaching of the true mark according to the Hīnayāna; thus, impermanence itself is the true mark.
The non-duality of permanence and impermanence is the true mark (*dharmatā*). To speak of permanence while being detached from permanence [is the meaning];
the four subsequent meanings, beginning with arising and ceasing, should be understood accordingly. Regarding the meaning of suffering as the true mark:
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi-sūtra* (Siyi jing) states:
"To know that suffering is non-arising is the Noble Truth of Suffering.
The *Mahāvaipulya-sūtra* states:
Ordinary beings have suffering but lack the Truth; those of the Two Vehicles have both suffering and the Truth.
Bodhisattvas understand that suffering is non-suffering;
yet, the meaning of "True Truth" (satya) is always the ultimate reality (dharmatā).
Because these five meanings regarding "great" and "small" are difficult to clarify, I shall briefly provide one illustration.
It is like a mother raising ten thousand children who, seeing them weeping incessantly, becomes fearful and says, "A ghost has come!
Those under one year of age do not fear hearing of a ghost.
This metaphor illustrates how ordinary people, upon hearing that the five aggregates are non-existent and so forth, do not feel revulsion toward them for five years.
After two or three years have passed, they become terrified upon hearing of ghosts;
this metaphor illustrates how those of the Two Vehicles feel revulsion and seek liberation upon hearing of impermanence and other such truths.
When he reached the age of fifteen, he heard it said that ghosts had come; yet ghosts fundamentally do not exist, they are merely conventional designations used because a child cries.

This serves as a metaphor for how a Bodhisattva realizes that the aggregates (skandhas) are without arising and are nothing but suffering and so forth, which are merely the Tathāgata’s provisional names and skillful means used to guide sentient beings.
Therefore, this is the true meaning: Aniruddha is translated in the Qin language as "As One Wishes" (Ruyi),
also called "Without Poverty," or "Without Extinction."
In the past, he once gave a single meal to a pratyekabuddha; for ninety-one kalpas thereafter, he constantly received the retribution of his wishes while dwelling in the heavens.
Thus it is called "Yongyi" (Wish-fulfilling).
Because he was perpetually free from poverty, it is called "Wupin" (Free from Poverty).
Because the roots of goodness are not extinguished, it is said they are "without extinction. Furthermore,
it is said that by entering a Buddhist stupa and trimming a lamp to illuminate it, the roots of goodness from ninety-one kalpas are not extinguished.
Now, having attained the retribution of the divine eye, it is said that there is no extinction. Regarding the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) and so forth:
if a *śrāvaka* gives rise to these powers based on the four dhyāna concentrations...

If there were unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) characterized by merit that could be perceived, then non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and others would also possess such perception; however, this is not the case.
If a śrāvaka, relying on wisdom (*prajñā*), abandons the afflictions (*kleśa*), this is termed "cessation through deliberation" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), which is an unconditioned phenomenon.
There should be no [dualistic] seeing;
the celestial eye of the Mahāyāna perceives forms within the Middle Way,
observing the three truths in their entirety and viewing both the provisional and the ultimate simultaneously.
It is quiescent yet illuminating;
therefore, this objection does not apply,
as will be self-evident from the text below.
The great and the small follow different paths, and between them there is this vast distinction.
Yet some, with their limited perspectives based on proximity and distance, attempt to differentiate the great from the small by means of quantitative measures;
is this not a grave error?
Furthermore, because the Buddha’s mind is entirely quiescent, his illumination sees nothing that is not seen.
Since wisdom is not separate from meditative concentration, it is quiescence itself while illuminating;
thus, seeing and [quiescence] are non-dual. Upāli addressed the Foremost One, saying:
It is also called "taking what is near.
Because the eight original śrāvakas took charge of administrative affairs and handled matters of giving and receiving, it is termed "near-attachment" and "near-taking.
As for the term "foremost leader":

This refers to the fact that when he went forth into homelessness at the same time as the eight śrāmaṇeras, the Tathāgata ordained him first, making him the senior elder (sthavira). Regarding the practice of the Vinaya, there are two types:
first, that which is originally unoffended.
The second involves repenting for transgressions;
this is the Vinaya practice of Upāli.
Now, Vimalakīrti takes the true nature of the Dharmakāya—originally pure, yet returning to awakening from the delusion of the fundamental faculties—as his Vinaya practice.
Therefore, a sutra says:
"Only the Buddha alone abides in the precepts; all others are called those who defile the precepts.
Furthermore, the text below says:
This is what constitutes fulfillment.
It clarifies that the *dharma-nature* (*dharmatā*) of this sutra’s precepts (*śīla*) fulfills the ten thousand practices through single-mindedness;
how could it be said to be fulfilled by merely two hundred and fifty [precepts]? Regarding "further increasing":

In the repentance methods of the Hīnayāna, it is required that one deeply perceive the accumulation of transgressions and give rise to a heart of profound regret; thus, they speak of "extinguishing" [the offenses].
Therefore, both the masters of Guanzhong and Tiantai state that when one turns one's back on the truth and commits delusions, these constitute the defilements of sin.
With sincere remorse and fear, my sense of shame increases all the more.
Now I offer this single explanation:
the intrinsic nature of sin is neither born nor extinguished.
In the past, when two people committed an offense, the failure to recognize it as such was called the "first offense.
Now, although Upāli has performed repentance for an offense that is not extinguished, he claims it is extinguished;
this is called "repeatedly increasing [the gravity of the offense]."
If this sin was originally unarisen,
then even now there is no extinction through repentance;
it is already removed and extinguished.
The *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-dhyāna-sūtra* states:
"If one wishes to perform repentance, one should seek the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
This true reality is the realization that both sin and the mind are equally non-extinguished."
This is called "upholding the Vinaya.
Is it not marvelous! As for the ninth liberation, it involves the abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation;
in each of the nine stages, there are nine unimpeded knowledges (*ānantarya-jñāna*) and nine liberations (*vimokṣa*).
Now, even in the ninth liberation within the stage of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one attains the mind-holding of an adept (aśaikṣa);
how much more so for the nature of the minds of sentient beings, which is fundamentally pure?
If delusive thoughts (*vikalpa*) were defilements, they would already be [delusive] thoughts.
To perceive impurity as impurity, or purity as impurity,
and likewise to grasp at a self through inversion,
is like a person with diseased eyes seeing flowers [in the sky].
When the illness is cured, one immediately realizes that the substance of the flower was originally non-existent.
Thus, Master Sheng said:
"The monk who seeks the truth clarifies that truth is not a fixed reality. As for "ceaseless arising and ceasing":
Now, one who commits a transgression cannot do so in a single thought-moment.
If a transgression is formed through the accumulation of thought-moments,
then each thought-moment itself arises and ceases, not abiding for even a single kṣaṇa.
How could it be considered a fault?
Furthermore, if mindfulness were not accumulated,
then even a single moment of thought would be without a cause.
If mindfulness were to abide and accumulate, it would not be a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
Furthermore, even if a single moment were to exist of its own accord,
the sinner does not abide for even a single *kṣaṇa*.
How could it be that through confession it is extinguished again? This is called one who upholds the Vinaya.
This *dharmatā-śīla* (precept of the nature of phenomena) is the very self-nature of the *dharmakāya*.
A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva maintains it in this manner. Rāhula is here translated as "the Obstructor."
This also demonstrates that he was foremost in secret practice. Regarding his renunciation of the position of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*):
when a Wheel-Turning King rules the world, the entire nation practices the ten wholesome paths of action.
How could he possibly abandon these manifold virtues to pursue only his own personal virtue?
Regarding the benefits and merits of leaving the household life (*pravrajyā*),
some speak of the benefit of "cutting away the thorns.
As stated in the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*:
Provided that they are śramaṇas by nature— even if their conduct defiles the form of a śramaṇa— and are śramaṇas who wear the kāṣāya robe,
they shall attain nirvāṇa without remainder under Maitreya Buddha and continuing on until Ruci Buddha.
Tiantai says:

Rāhula spoke of the ten knowledges, the three insights, and other benefits obtained through the four fruits [of the śrāvaka path]. Regarding "no benefit and no merit," I have privately investigated that there are briefly three distinctions among those who have left the household life.
First, renouncing craving and one's retinue is called "leaving home.
Second, severing both views and cultivation to exit the prison of the triple world is called "leaving home.
Third, profoundly awakening to the Mahāyāna.
Birth-and-death and nirvana are neither bondage nor liberation;
outflows and the absence of outflows are neither defiled nor pure;
there is no grasping and no relinquishing, no attainment and no realization.
To realize that the dharma-realm is like an illusion and to awaken to the true nature that is free from dependence is called the ultimate Mahāyāna true renunciation.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Because there is nothing to be attained, one attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This is the renunciation of the Great Being Vimalakīrti, which is without gain and without merit.
Is it not so that Rāhula, by abandoning the faults and afflictions of the three realms and attaining the merit of nirvāṇa, is called a true renunciant?
As for "provisional names," both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are merely provisional names.
Therefore, the subsequent text states:
"Both 'self' and 'nirvāṇa'—these two are both empty.
By what are they empty?
It is merely empty because its own name is [empty]. Regarding "one who has emerged from the mud":
for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), the five desires constitute the mud;
for those of the two vehicles (*dvayayānika*), the attainment of realization constitutes the mud. The "four graspings" (*catvāra upādānāni*) are the four types of sensation (*vedanā*).
It is further said:
"He does not accept the three realms nor nirvana. Ānanda means "Joy" in this language;
Ānanda was born again on the night the Buddha attained the Way.
He was named by his father, the king, because his birth brought joy.
Furthermore, he was so named because those who saw him rejoiced due to the roots of goodness from his past lives. "Do not slander the Tathāgata."
The Hīnayāna asserts that the Buddha is a body born of karma, manifesting in form to achieve enlightenment.

The Mahāyāna maintains that one realizes the body is fundamentally non-existent as a body; it is the Dharma-body (dharmakāya), which manifests in response to sentient beings as a trace-body (nirmāṇakāya).
This is simply responding to conditions as if it were an illness, rather than being a real illness.
To now insist that it is truly summoned by karma—
is this not slander?
The various teachings speak of the "golden spear," "barley," and so forth; these examples are to be understood in the same way.
Regarding the statement that this is the *dharmakāya*:
in the Hīnayāna, the sixteen-foot form is regarded as the body of birth and death (*saṃsāra-kāya*).
The fivefold dharma constitutes the Dharma-body.
In the Mahāyāna, form is itself emptiness;
the six-foot [Buddha] is itself the Real.
The Real is the eternally abiding nature of phenomena (dharmatā);
it is not produced by the karma of thought.
It is identical with the aggregates (skandhas) and identical with emptiness (śūnyatā), and it transcends the three realms.
Emptiness is itself purity;
what outflows could there be?
The four marks are in constant flux.
Arising and ceasing lack intrinsic nature;
thus, they are both shifting and non-shifting.
Therefore, it is called the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). "All numbers" refers to the enumeration of the four characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*).
Yuan said: "Those who are not subject to thought and desire sever the afflictive hindrances;
those who transcend the three realms leave behind the fruit of segmented existence."
The "outflow-free" (anāsrava) destroys the cognitive obstructions (jñeyāvaraṇa);
the "unconditioned" (asaṃskṛta) is free from the fruit of transformation (pariṇāmiphala). Chongfu said:
It is not produced by volition or desire, nor is it born of karma,
because its arising is sovereign.
This is my transcendence of the three realms.
The three realms are suffering.
To transcend the suffering of the three realms is bliss.
This is the untainted.
The outflows are defilement;
the absence of outflows is purity.
As for the unconditioned:
Conditioned phenomena are impermanent;
the Buddha-body is unconditioned and is therefore permanent. As the layman has said, the true permanence of the Buddha-body is as previously explained.
This reveals the ultimate truth (*tattva*).

Not being born in the five turbidities (*pañca-kāṣāya*) while manifesting illness to benefit sentient beings—this opens up the provisional means (*upāya*). It is not said that he does not manifest; rather, one should understand that clinging to the body of illness as real is the sickness, whereas hearing of this illness clarifies that the body is not the self (*anātman*).
Therein lies the opening of the provisional.
However, the body is not "mine";
it exists only because it serves as a vessel for all things.
Because beings possess bodies,
that which is the body is itself not the body; it is the Dharma-body.
This also reveals the reality.
Such is the scriptural text;
the principle is likewise clear.
Yet those who are deluded claim that it is only upon reaching the Lotus Sūtra that the provisional is opened and the real is revealed,
and that it is only upon reaching the Nirvāṇa Sūtra that the Dharma-body of one's own person is finally expounded.
Is this not a mistaken reading of the scriptural texts?
Furthermore, the Lotus Sūtra also states that for the sake of the five turbidities, the One Vehicle is opened up into the Three Vehicles;
likewise, this sūtra also reveals the Dharma-body as a "sick body" for the sake of the five turbidities.
What difference is there between knowing that the three are false and realizing that they are a sickness?
What distinction is there between awakening to the three as one and perceiving that the response is itself the truth?
Furthermore, the Mahāyāna Sūtra also says:
"This body of mine is now the eternal body, the Dharma-body.
This sutra also says:
"The Buddha-body is the Dharma-body."
Furthermore, it is said:
"The Buddha-body is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and does not fall within the realm of numerical categories.
How could one possibly discern its unconditioned nature apart from this sixteen-foot form?"
Yet those who stagnate in the teachings and lose their essential intent, upon reaching the *Lotus Sūtra*, cling to the "one vehicle" and the "one principle," asserting that other sūtras are not one;
when they reach the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and learn that the Reward Buddha is eternal, they immediately claim that all other teachings are not eternal.
How could the Dharma-gate of non-duality not be the single true mark of *prajñā* and not be eternal?
Thus we know that when one exhausts the source and reaches the ultimate,
the principle cannot be different.
The teachings manifested according to the faculties of beings cannot be uniform;
names and teachings have no fixed definition, clarifying that the principle is fundamentally nameless.
How can one cling to names under the guise of "the nameless" and thereby become fettered by dogmatic views?
The five turbidities (pañca kaṣāyāḥ) are also called the five dregs;
the names differ, but the meaning is one and the same.
First is the defilement of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*),
which refers to the perilous danger when the great and small three calamities occur.
Second is the defilement of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*).
The six realms of existence dwell together, bound by the suffering of karma;
this is the turbidity of the three afflictions,
for greed, anger, ignorance, and pride have increased to an extreme degree.
Fourth is the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*), in which the attachments to the view of a self, extreme views, false views, and so forth, are so firm as to be unshakable.
Fifth is the turbidity of lifespan (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*).
Lifespans are short and the cultivation of goodness is not accomplished.
The *Beihua jing* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra) clarifies that during the kalpas of formation, destruction, and emptiness, there is no turbidity;
it is only during the kalpa of abiding, when the human lifespan reaches twenty thousand years, that turbidity arises, continuing until it reaches sixty thousand years.
The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* mentions six turbidities (*kaṣāya*),
while the *Nirgrantha-sūtra* mentions twelve turbidities; thus,
the number of turbidities is not fixed.
One thus knows that at the end of the kalpa, the sages are remote;
for what is not turbid?
The mention of five, six, and so forth is merely the teaching distributed according to the faculties [of beings].
In the "Bodhisattva Chapter," since the preceding chapter already contained the words addressed by the śrāvakas,
it would have been logical to command the bodhisattvas next.
As for why they were not commanded first:
If a Great Being offers words of exhortation,
the life-force of a Śrāvaka is immediately stilled;
how could the path of introduction not be bestowed?
Tiantai’s exposition on the intention behind the Bodhisattva’s rebuke briefly sets forth five points:
to manifest the sublime virtues of Vimalakīrti and to turn [the assembly] toward the two types of expedient teachings.
Third, it swiftly accomplishes the Pure Land;
fourth, it serves as a skillful means for entering the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*;
fifth, it seals and confirms the formation of the sūtra.
First, regarding the manifestation of his virtue:
although the śrāvakas previously praised him, it was like the strength of a child lifting a bucket—it was not sufficient to be considered heroic.
Now, by the bodhisattvas bowing in submission, the virtue of Vimalakīrti is truly revealed.
The Great Being is honored as a model; his teachings can be put into practice.
How could he be superior or inferior to ordinary people?
Second, there are those who, having received the gradual teachings, enter the gate of the perfect and subtle Bodhisattvas.
The Bodhisattvas share the same consciousness, yet their profound teachings differ.
The *Abhidharmakośa* states:

"For three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, he practiced the six pāramitās; for one hundred kalpas, he cultivated the causes for the marks and signs; then, descending from Tuṣita, he manifested the eight phases of enlightenment, beginning with sitting beneath the tree of awakening."
Thus, it is through thirty-four moments of mind that an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) finally achieves perfect enlightenment;
this is the ultimate consciousness.
The *Dapin jing* (Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra) explains that the ten stages (bhūmi) are practiced in common by the three vehicles (triyāna).
The followers of the two vehicles sever [afflictions] and realize [the fruit];
the Bodhisattvas sever them but do not realize [the fruit].

These are: the stage of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi*), the stage of external ordinary beings (*bāhya-pṛthagjana-bhūmi*), the stage of internal ordinary beings (*adhyātma-pṛthagjana-bhūmi*), the stage of the eight persons (*aṣṭamaka-bhūmi*), the stage of the candidate for the first fruit (*pratipannaka-prathamaphala-bhūmi*), the eighth person’s stage of vision (*darśana-bhūmi*), the stage of the first fruit (*prathamaphala-bhūmi*), the stage of attenuation (*tanu-bhūmi*), the stage of the second fruit (*dvitīyaphala-bhūmi*) for those who have abandoned desire, the stage of the third fruit (*tritīyaphala-bhūmi*), the stage of the fourth fruit (*caturthaphala-bhūmi*) for those who have completed what was to be done, the stage of the Pratyekabuddha, the stage of the Bodhisattva, and the stage of the Buddha.
This means that while the three vehicles equally contemplate non-arising (*anutpāda*), there are differences in the depth of their realization.
The three animals crossing the river and the three arrows hitting the cauldron are all metaphors for this;
the present case represents the profound level.
By departing from the views of the three vehicles,
one cultivates and perfects *Awakened Awareness* through the fifty-two stages of the *Benevolent Kings’ Garland Sūtra*,
beginning with the ten levels of faith (*śraddhā*).
That there is but one Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) with no other categories is even more profound.

Because of the many gates of stages and practices, and the distinctions arising from diverse terminology, it appears as different; yet it is neither manifold nor singular—it is the inconceivable, perfectly wondrous Way.
The *Huayan* says:
"One who studies in this manner does not proceed from one stage to another, but rather fully possesses all dharmas within the stages.
The *Laṅkāvatāra* says:
What sequence is there for quiescent true suchness?
A great sutra states:
"On the Snowy Mountains there is a herb called 'Patience.'"
If a cow eats [this], it can produce ghee (*sarpis*);
it is not a gradual transformation of milk or curd.
This sutra says:
To know all dharmas in a single thought is the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), for it accomplishes all-knowledge (sarvajñatā).
In one stage are all stages; in one practice are all practices.
A single hair’s breadth of goodness initiates one's departure and halts at the Buddha;
it is neither round nor partial, yet it is provisionally designated as the Perfect and Sudden Mahāyāna.
In the past, the various great beings received transformation according to their faculties, and through their differing attachments, they fell into delusion.

The Buddha’s ultimate, perfect, and wondrous Great Way is now being probed and rebuked by the Great Being Vimalakīrti, who causes all partial views to be relinquished and gradually opens the way for complete understanding.
This suddenly establishes the path of inconceivable liberation.
Regarding the third point, the three joys that constitute the seven meanings of the Tathāgata’s true purity:
heretofore, the various Bodhisattvas have each adhered to partial and shallow interpretations.
That is to say, while the world of Sahā is certainly defiled and the realm of King Lamp-King is certainly pure,
there is no one who does not loathe the defiled and rejoice in the pure;
yet because their attachment and clinging are profound, they remain ever more distant from the Way.
Now, Vimalakīrti’s censure was intended to make known that impurity and purity are non-dual and not distinct.
Thus, Ānanda’s subsequent awakening to the Buddha-work and the monks of the Fragrant Accumulation World’s repentance for having seen the impure realms were both in accordance with this intent.
Fourth, regarding those who enter the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and *Nirvāṇa* as a skillful means for their spiritual lineage:

since the various great beings were unable to attain sudden enlightenment into the perfect and subtle [truth] and instead each followed partial and gradual teachings, Vimalakīrti now refutes those of sharp faculties so that they may realize and enter [the truth] in this very seat; this was previously included in the second section.

Those of dull faculties who rely on various conditions first undergo censure and later attain realization and entry by hearing such teachings as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and the *Nirvāṇa* sūtras.
It was precisely because he was rebuked and chastised that he subsequently attained awakening.
Thus, the *Dharmadhātuprakṛti-śāstra* states:
"If a person of sharp faculties enters the dharmadhātu through the Mahāprajñāpāramitā..."
If those of medium capacity enter the Dharma-realm through the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*,
those of inferior capacity enter the Dharma-realm through *nirvāṇa*.
Thus we know that those who awaken through the initial teaching of the *Avataṃsaka* enter [the Dharma-realm] within the "milk" teaching.
Next, within the Āgamas, one awakens to the teaching of curd and enters it;
within this sutra and the various Vaipulya sutras, one awakens to the teachings of clarified butter (*sarpis*) and enters them;

within the *Prajñāpāramitā* which serves as a barrier to the Dharma, one awakens to the teaching of ghee (*ghṛta*) and enters it; and finally, within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Nirvāṇa*, one enters the ultimate essence of *amṛta* (the "cream of ghee").
Fifth, regarding the sealing and authentication of the sutra:
previously, the words of the *ākhyāna* had not received formal authorization;
now, they are proclaimed before the Buddha.
Having received the seal of approval from the Tathāgata,
it became the cause for the Dharma teachings to flow forth and reach far and wide. Maitreya is translated here as "Miaozhi" (慈氏),
which refers to his clan name.
He is named Ajita, which means "Unconquerable. As for those who practice non-retrogression:
because the gods of Tuṣita in the Desire Realm are attached to pleasure, they frequently undergo retrogression.
Therefore, Maitreya expounded the practice of non-retrogression.
Where there is both progress and retrogression,
one is subject to the preferences of partial teachings— either aversion or aspiration.
Neither advancing nor retreating, it is that which transcends all dependence.
Now, Vimalakīrti uses this state of non-retreat to refute Maitreya’s advance and retreat based on dependence.
Regarding those who possess clear discernment,
there are four types of non-retrogression.
The first is non-retrogression in principle.
First, because their essential nature and characteristics are eternally abiding.
Second, there is non-retrogression from the stage [of practice],
because they do not regress into the vehicles of the two types of śrāvakas or into external paths.
Third is non-retrogression in practice,
because wisdom realizes non-arising.
Fourth is non-retrogression in mindfulness.
Because it is quiescent yet constantly active;
as for the statement that the seeds of the sublime marks are the cause for non-retrogression, this refers exclusively to non-retrogression in terms of stage (*avasthā*).
Practicing the ten stages together, the stage of the nature of the ground constitutes non-retrogression in position;
the stage of insight constitutes non-retrogression in practice.
In the gradual teaching, these four types of non-retrogression are individually established.
Prior to the arousal of the ten faiths, there is non-retrogression in principle;
at the stage of the ten abidings, there is non-retrogression in position; and at the first bhūmi, there is non-retrogression in practice.
In the eighth stage, one does not regress through mindfulness;
in the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), all four types of non-regression are fully present.
Now, the Great Being (Mahāsattva) frequently uses "non-regression" as a point of difficulty. As for the master carver from Ying:
This account originates from the *Zhuangzi*. It says:
"A man of Ying had plaster smeared over his nose."
When the artisan Shi wielded his adze with the force of a wind,
he removed the plaster without even scratching his nose; drawing from this,
although the mental artisan may be able to wield such skill, [it remains a matter of craft].
One must necessarily rely on the immovable substance of a person from Jing;
although Vimalakīrti was able to play the lute, it was also required that Maitreya be able to receive it. As for those who cross arms:
Zhuangzi said: He addressed Yan Hui, saying,
"I shall join arms with you for the rest of our lives."

As for the meaning of the words "impermanent" and "ever-changing," they refer to the mutual succession of every thought-moment. When it speaks of "bestowing a prediction of enlightenment" (*vyākaraṇa*), it means that the nature of awakening is truly eternal, being neither something accomplished nor something attained;
the mention of bestowing a prediction is intended to guide those who have not yet realized this truth.
If one hears the prediction and becomes attached to it, this constitutes an attainment that is not a true attainment of the prediction.
It is not as good as awakening to the fact that the essence of the aggregates is empty; such "non-attainment" is what is called the true prediction.
Vajrapāṇi said:
"I did not obtain even the slightest dharma from the Buddha Dīpaṃkara;
yet the Buddha Dīpaṃkara bestowed upon me a prediction of enlightenment."
If one were to differentiate them,
as stated in the Śūraṅgama Sūtra,
there are four kinds of prophecy (vyākaraṇa).
First, bestowing a prediction of enlightenment upon one who has not yet generated the aspiration;
second, bestowing a prediction in secret;
third, bestowing a prediction in the presence of others.
Regarding the four views on non-arising,
three of the former receive predictions of enlightenment,
while the latter one does not receive a prediction.
Now, the Great Being rebukes the prior state of having attainment;
he now accords with the subsequent state of non-attainment. Those who abandon the view of discriminating bodhi will experience both progress and regression, as well as attainment and non-attainment.

When acceptance and rejection alternate and the wills of joy and aversion diverge, these are all views that differentiate within bodhi; they are not the true vision. Regarding "that which cannot be attained by means of the body":
this is a skillful teaching intended for bodhisattvas who believe they attain bodhisattvahood by means of a body endowed with the marks and signs (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana).
When the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows and the knowledge of non-arising are attained by the mind, one becomes a Bodhisattva; all such categories are likewise.
This is the definitive explanation.
A body possessing marks is not bodhi;
a mind possessing cognition is not bodhi.
It is better to realize that within marks there are no marks, and within the mind there is no arising.
Both are quiescent;
this very quiescence is bodhi,
for it extinguishes all marks.
"Various characteristics" refers to the four characteristics of arising, abiding, change, and cessation.
All the following phrases are established precisely through such refutation. "The profound path that transcends and drives ahead" means:
Illuminating the profound course, the myriad practices transcend all;
riding alone toward the state of ultimate evenness, yet without perceiving the mark of evenness. As for the "Radiantly Adorned Bodhimanda": [it is as follows].
This secluded dwelling amidst forests and springs is a site of spiritual practice; when the awakened mind is realized,
it is itself the truth.
This is the true field for awakening to principle.
Moreover, a single moment of an evil thought suddenly deludes the dharma-realm;
yet by turning back from delusion, one attains the real, and the myriad practices are eternally pure.
This means that by realizing the single mind, the myriad practices are themselves the true path; by awakening to a single speck of dust, the entire dharma-realm becomes a perfectly pure field.
How could one treat this casually as a mere place of practice? It is when wisdom directly perceives all phenomena that it constitutes a site of enlightenment.
When deluded consciousness grasps at signs, it deviates from reality and clings to the false;
this is not called "direct perception.
When correct wisdom illuminates the principle, it reverses the false and attains the real.
This is called "direct perception. Regarding the statement that "in a single thought-moment one knows all dharmas":
the Hīnayāna explains this through the truth of the Four Noble Truths as the cessation of opposing categories, wherein there is suffering to be loathed and afflictions to be severed.
Therefore, one attains Buddhahood through thirty-four moments of mind.
In the Mahāyāna, because not even a single color or a single fragrance is not the Middle Way, and because a single thought-moment and a single wisdom simultaneously encompass all practices,
one is able to know [all things] within a single instant.
This is inconceivable wisdom;
how could those thirty-four moments of mind be conceivable wisdom?
As for what is called "the thirty-four moments of mind":
This is from the Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya:
After the Tathāgata had defeated the armies of Māra beneath the Bodhi tree,
he severed the afflictions of the path of seeing by means of the eight knowledges and the eight patiences.
The nine unimpeded knowledges (*anantarya-jñāna*) and the nine liberations (*vimokṣa*) are what are cultivated;

hence it is said there are thirty-four. In reality, however, the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*) pertain to the nine stages (*bhūmi*) across the three realms (*dhātu*).
Each of the nine grades of the stages (*bhūmi*) has nine unhindered knowledges (*ānantarya-jñāna*) and nine liberations (*vimokṣa*).
Thus, there are eighty-one grades of unhindered knowledge and eighty-one grades of liberation.
Now, those that each reside in one grade are only the characteristics of a single stage.
Because the outflowing dharmas (*sāsrava-dharma*) of the eight stages below this have already been abandoned;

as for "the world-abider dwelling in tranquility," this refers to the attachment to the non-cultivation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) by bodhisattvas through various skillful means (*upāya*).
However, to abandon clamor and seek stillness seems to contradict the principle of equality;
therefore, Vimalakīrti rebuked [Śāriputra]. As for the identity of the two realms of Māra and Buddha within the single suchness of reality:
The realm of Māra is the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya),
while the realm of the Buddha is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
The Bodhisattva of skillful means has not yet fully realized the Middle Way.
Adapting to worldly conventions while turning one's back on the truth leads to delusion through attachment to the mundane;
when the illuminating mind comes and goes in this way, one enters the realm of Māra.
A Bodhisattva of the Perfect Teaching perfectly illumines the Middle Way.
The true and the conventional are of one suchness; through the equal contemplation of the three truths, one illuminates that there is no coming or going, and thus Māras cannot enter.
Therefore, the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* says:
In the world, there are those who constantly cultivate the sphere of empty space, wherein emptiness is eternally present amidst the myriad transformations;
this is precisely the meaning [of the teaching].
As for the second point, regarding the cultivation of contemplation through two conditions, there is an interval between entering and emerging.
This "True Cultivation of Conditions" originated during the Liang and Qi dynasties and was employed by Dharma Masters;
its principles are profound and subtle.
Therefore, Tiantai utilized it.
Regarding the cultivation based on the three conditions:
because cognition and its object are distinct,
the object is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
Wisdom is precisely *prajñā*.
This wisdom takes the ultimate truth as its object, eliminates delusions, and brings about the state of a noble one (*ārya*).
Apart from this wisdom, there exists the world of objects.
Regarding what is called "true cultivation":
because wisdom and its object are one, the ultimate truth is eternal;
being pure, it illuminates while remaining pure.
It is never impure;
it is never without illumination,
like a wish-fulfilling jewel.
The substance of the jewel is perfectly round and pure;
its pure light shines constantly.
It is both true and luminous.
Because defilements are constantly removed, it is called "true cultivation.
Therefore, for the Bodhisattva of Expedient Means, wisdom exists outside the realm;
because it illuminates only through intentional application, there are times when it does not illuminate.
In the interval before one has applied focused attention, Māra gains entry.

In the perfect and sudden true cultivation, where object and wisdom are identical and principle and illumination are non-dual, there is no coming or going in the contemplation of this illuminating principle; thus, Māra cannot enter.
"Māra" refers to the four māras:
first, the celestial māra (devaputramāra);
second, the māra of afflictions (kleśamāra).
The third is the demon of the aggregates (skandhamāra), and the fourth is the demon of death (mṛtyumāra).
What is now called "demon" (māra) refers specifically to the celestial demon (devaputramāra).
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states that where there is no permanence, bliss, self, or purity, there is Māra;
and that which is Māra consists entirely of the affliction-māras (*kleśamāra*). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:
"Except for the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*), everything else is the work of Māra."

One should immediately emerge from the path and correctly contemplate that all external deluded thoughts are the works of Māra. Regarding the cultivation of the three enduring dharmas—body, life, and wealth—this refers to the endurance of the body, the endurance of life, and the endurance of wealth.
There are four levels of depth regarding these three firm things (*tri-dṛḍha*).
First, the three firm things of the world:
by not harming the bodies of others, by saving the sick, and by giving food, one attains the firmness of the body.
By not taking the lives of others and by practicing the release of life and the cessation of killing, one attains firmness of life.
By not stealing the wealth of others and by practicing generosity without stinginess, one attains firmness of wealth.
These are the two forms of firmness for śrāvakas.

Through diligent cultivation of the untainted (anāsrava), one constantly contemplates impermanence and attains the fivefold Dharma-body, the untainted life-force of wisdom, and the seven treasures of the noble ones' Dharma;
these cannot be destroyed or impaired. Thus it is said.
The three skillful means teach the Bodhisattva’s three firmnesses:
the Dharma-body of True Suchness is indestructible like a diamond;
the life-force of Prajñā-wisdom is observed as never subject to cessation.
The wealth of the myriad wholesome dharmas is perfectly cultivated without deficiency;
this is the third sitting of the Bodhisattva.
Fourth is Perfect Enlightenment, the Three Firmnesses.
That is to say, the true permanence of the dharma-nature is itself quiescence.
It constantly contemplates and illuminates the myriad virtues and merits of all phenomena as being truly real.
These three "firmnesses" (susthita) are three in one and one in three; they are neither three nor one, yet they can manifest as three and can manifest as one.
Therefore, the Great Sūtra says:
"The Mahāprajñā, liberation, and the Dharma-body are neither vertical nor horizontal, neither identical nor different.
Prajñā is the life-force of wisdom.
Liberation is the wealth of the Dharma;
the Dharma-body is the true body.
This is what is called the ultimate, eternally abiding triad of the firm. As for things that are not of the Dharma:
A woman is a condition for the destruction of the Path;
it is said so because she is specifically what Bodhi fears.

It also indicates that the Bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings have not yet realized the underlying principle, and thus they were rebuked by Vimalakīrti. As for "Śramaṇa," it was formerly transliterated as [Sanskrit characters].
This is called "abundant merit. To speak of "exertion in the cultivation of the Way" means that it is laborious.
Furthermore, to speak of "diligent toil" signifies the meaning of sincere resolve; this is termed "resting."
Next, one attains the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*) where birth and death come to rest; it is also called "Pure Resolve" (*śuddhādhyāśaya*).
Regarding "bowing and looking up": "bowing" means lowering the head, while "looking up" means raising the head.

As for the statement, "She remained silent and did not persist in forcing herself upon me; I have already renounced her," this clarifies that the Great Being constantly abides in the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*), such that his dharmas and vows are fully perfected.

When the woman heard the Dharma, her dharmas were fulfilled; by complying with the Māra's wish, his vow was fulfilled. As for the question, "How did she come to rest within the palace of Māra? [it is as follows:]

The disciple understands the Master’s principle and requests instruction: "The 'Inexhaustible Lamp' is not merely a single illumination; when it comes as clarity, it is the Dharma-joy for one's own benefit, while as the Inexhaustible Lamp, it serves to transform others."
This is precisely the perfection of the practices for the dual benefit [of self and others], constantly benefiting beings throughout the past and future;
herein lies the presence of unimpeded, wondrous eloquence. As for "well-obtained" (*sukṛta*) and also "well-bestowed" (*suvihita*), these refer to the sublime realization of the Mahāsattva.
Which practice is not perfected?
Nevertheless, because each attracts beings according to its own gate, each has its own excellence.
He skillfully attained his mark in the matter of giving, being without stinginess.
Yet, being unable to exhaustively fathom the source of giving or to skillfully penetrate the myriad practices, he was thus enlightened by Vimalakīrti through the Dharma.
Furthermore, this is likely a case of call-and-response; how could it be said to be anything other than that?
Regarding those who establish great assemblies for giving:
in the past, their parents practiced the rites of heterodox shrines,
or they slaughtered oxen, sheep, humans, and so forth to sacrifice to the heavens in pursuit of blessings.
Shandei resided there under a deceptive guise;
he redirected the offerings of the heterodox shrine toward righteous giving,
yet he was unable to immediately implement the practice of enshrining [the relics] to perform the great Dharma-giving.
Therefore, Vimalakīrti used reproof as a means to penetrate this truth.
As in the *Abhidharmakośa*,
during the period of the Hīnayāna, Bodhisattvas practice the six perfections through skillful means.
In all cases, the fulfillment of the six perfections is achieved by not begrudging either wealth or one's own life.
Now, in the Mahāyāna, the practice of the six perfections is entirely in accord with the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
Abiding in the vow of great compassion within the equality of the true limit and the sameness of the dharma-nature,
one bestows even a single hair’s breadth of merit equally upon all sentient beings so that they may together realize bodhi;
this is called the perfection of the gift of Dharma.
Therefore, a verse in the Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya says: "Out of compassion, he gave universally;
though his body was mangled, he felt no anger;
he praised Buddha Tiṣya."
This is because unsurpassed bodhi is perfected through the non-sparing of body and life.
The Vajra Sūtra says:
"One should practice giving without dwelling on form."
Even to the point of having one's body cut to pieces, there is no self and no person.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states:
"The *dāna-pāramitā* is pure."
The purity of all-knowledge is non-dual and undifferentiated;
even so is the purity of wisdom.
This accords with principle and realizes the true mark (*dharmatā*).
Its merit rescues all sentient beings;
in accordance with principle, one practices giving and gives rise to vows according to their capacities.
Therefore, it is called "perfection.

Now, Vimalakīrti criticizes the six perfections within the preceding matters in order to lead people into the six perfections of the subsequent true reality (*dharmatā*). Regarding "upholding the True Dharma and giving rise to a mind of sympathetic joy":
This mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) is also the joy of the Dharma;
it causes both oneself and others who uphold the Dharma to practice this mind of sympathetic joy.
Furthermore, because both uphold the True Dharma together, they equally attain the joy of the Dharma. As for "great equanimity" (*mahopekṣā*), it is the relinquishing of all things.
The Mahāsattva of Expedient Means abandons both enemy and kin,
and likewise abandons the immeasurable minds.
The Mahāsattva of Perfect Suddenness abandons all phenomena.
This is what is called "immeasurable relinquishment.

It is also called "relinquishment" because one practices until reaching the ultimate reality (*dharmatā*). Regarding "arousing diligence while remaining free from the marks of body and mind," there are two interpretations.

One interpretation states: when the single mind does not awaken to the fact that there is no path outside of itself, and both body and mind perish such that one receives the name of "vigor," this is [ordinary] vigor.
When it accords with the principle of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) and abides eternally within true reality, such that the characteristics of body and mind are empty, this is called "true vigor."
The arising of a mind with signs is precisely what is called indolence;
therefore, it is said that [this practice] arises by being free from the signs of body and mind. Question:

All treatises state that the essence of the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*) consists of the factor of "diligence" (*vīrya*) among the eleven wholesome mental factors (*caitta-dharma*), together with the three types of action (*karman*) that accompany it.
Up to and including generosity (*dāna*), which takes the perfection of giving (*tyāga-pāramitā*) and the three modes of conduct—body, speech, and mind—as its essential substance;
these six perfections, in their fundamental nature, do not transcend the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of body and mind.
Question: Why is it said here that the characteristic of diligence is free from grasping at body and mind?
Answer: This is not logically tenable.
Why is this? Because the profound Mahāyāna sūtras require one to exhaustively investigate the names and numbers of the five aggregates (*skandha*) as they truly are.

Since the Buddha perceived that non-Buddhists initially adhered to false conceptions regarding arising, he taught the Dharma of correct causes and conditions through the enumeration of the aggregates (*skandha*) and elements (*dhātu*).
The Buddha guides those of the two vehicles to eliminate the view of self;
how can one explain the profound and subtle [teachings] while still harboring biased and limited views?
Furthermore, for the sake of those of the two vehicles, the Buddha taught the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense bases (āyatanas).
I wish to cause them to realize that the wisdom of the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya) is conditioned and impermanent;
nor do I wish to cause them to cling to the enumeration of phenomena—whether many or few—as being real.
If one clings to them as real, one moves further away from the Path.
Furthermore, when the Mahāyāna explains the dharmas of the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), and sense-bases (āyatana),
it likewise intends not to establish these dharmas as real entities. Why is this?
If dharmas were definitively the five aggregates,
one should not speak of the twelve bases;
if they were definitively the twelve bases...
One should not speak of eighteen elements;
five and eight have no fixed number.
One should know that this is both number and non-number.
The aggregates and elements have no fixed characteristics;
one should know that characteristics are non-characteristics.
The aggregates and elements have no fixed names.
One should know that names are nameless;
thus, the preceding passage states:
"Dharmas have no form or characteristics, being like empty space."
Therefore, phenomena have no names, because words and language are cut off.
These are all taken as signless precisely by virtue of their signs;
thus they are called "nameless."
This is precisely to seek in accordance with the sūtras, not by seeking for form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
not by seeking for the elements (dhātus) or the sense bases (āyatanas).
This constitutes the true seeking of the Dharma.
If one reasons in this manner,
how can the actual substance of the six perfections be discerned through the names and numbers of the aggregates and elements?
For one who seeks the truth:
One should distance oneself from the characteristics of body and mind and seek [the truth] within the true mark (dharmatā).
I pray that students will carefully examine its significance. Regarding the statement, "To teach and transform sentient beings, one gives rise to emptiness, etc.":
If one follows the Hīnayāna and various treatises, the three samādhis are explained as having the sixteen aspects of the Four Noble Truths as their object;
however, the Mahāyāna sūtras explain that the causal conditions for the three samādhis are the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
This is in perfect agreement with the scriptural text.
Why? Because the Four Noble Truths of the Mahāyāna are precisely the Four Noble Truths of non-arising.
In both cases, the non-arising of suffering, its origin, and so forth is taken as the truth;
it is not suffering and its origin themselves that are taken as the truth.
If one takes the non-arising of suffering, its origin, and so forth as the truth, [then...]
The truths are the conditions for the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
This true mark gives rise to the three samādhis,
which is what fundamentally distinguishes [this teaching] from the Hīnayāna.
As for the scriptural passage stating that "the transformation of the multitudes gives rise to emptiness" and so forth:
because the illumination of the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) perfects both provisional and ultimate wisdom,
that which is transformed is itself empty.

"To dwell in emptiness while constantly transforming" means that because emptiness and existence are non-dual, one simultaneously illuminates both the provisional and the real. "Not abandoning conditioned phenomena while giving rise to the signless" means that,
in the Lesser Vehicle, the extinction of the marks of the Truth of Cessation is considered the signless.
In the Mahāyāna, that which possesses characteristics is itself without characteristics;
this very absence of characteristics is called the true characteristic (bhūtalakṣaṇa).
Therefore, one does not abandon existence to become non-existent of itself. Manifesting birth while giving rise to the state of non-action.
In the Hīnayāna, the cessation of all purposeful activity is termed "non-action" (*anabhisamskāra*).
In the Mahāyāna, because the very essence of action is non-action, one acts throughout the day without seeking non-action.
This is the non-action of the inconceivable true reality (*tathatā*).
Even down to the "Inconceivable" chapter on the two dharma-gates, within a single gate of liberation, all three gates of liberation are identical.
This path accords with principle and is non-dual. Regarding the statement that "the practice of wholesome dharmas arises from pure livelihood" (*pariśuddhājīva*):
what is called "wrong livelihood" (*mithyājīva*) refers to sustaining one's life through improper gain.

If a practitioner, while grasping at the aggregates (*skandha*), seeks goodness, becomes attached to views, and gives rise to cultivation with a perverted mind, seeking goodness and desiring to sustain their livelihood through such means—all this is wrong livelihood.
If one correctly contemplates the Middle Way, this is the fundamental reality of all phenomena; therein,
myriad virtues are spontaneously perfected,
and merit remains eternally pure.
Since one neither grasps at signs nor seeks profit to sustain the spirit, it is called "pure livelihood" (*pariśuddhājīva*).
Regarding the phrase "to untie the bonds of sentient beings and give rise to the stages of practice":
the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is eternally quiescent, being neither shallow nor deep, yet the sūtras differ [in their expressions].
The exposition of the stages and positions according to their depth and shallowness constitutes the sequence for initiating practice as a skillful means to attract sentient beings;
although this pertains to matters external to the nature of reality (dharmatā), it is nonetheless essential.
This refers to the stages of initiating practice.
Furthermore, it is said that because ultimate truth is neither shallow nor deep, there are no stages of cultivation.
Since delusion constitutes the conditioned fetters and bonds,
there is a sequence of stages in their unraveling.
To know all phenomena without grasping or rejecting them— this is [the path].
The commentary states:
"To engage the mind in discernment" means that by discerning appearances as being without appearance, one then enters the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
The characteristic of the true nature (*dharmatā*) is precisely the single characteristic.
This single characteristic is without characteristics; it is provisionally named "one" because it universally pervades all things. Regarding the donor’s impartial mind:
their reverence for the Buddha is profound.
Their giving to the poor is profound with compassion;
through their pure and deep compassion and their reverent sincerity and righteousness, they simultaneously destroy birth and death and attain Great Nirvana.
Therefore, it is said that they are equal in terms of the common characteristics of the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*). As for "being without discrimination":
The various marks being non-marks is the body of the Tathāgata.
The five aggregates are all empty, termed the substance of a poor man.
In the nonduality of the dharma-nature, both gift and retribution are extinguished.
Because one gives by means of this, there is no discrimination.
In the "Mañjuśrī’s Inquiry on the Sick" chapter (upper section), having already refuted dharmas and subdued [the opponent] through the three chapters outside the hall.
This is the inferior grade of governance through the embracing of the Dharma.
Thus, the Śrīmālā-sūtra states:
"Those who should be subdued, one should subdue."
One should embrace those who are worthy of being embraced;
because of this embracing through subduing, it is said that the True Dharma will abide for a long time.
Below, Tiantai briefly uses four meanings to provide a general explanation of the six chapters of the scripture.
First, clarifying the purpose of the visit;
second, clarifying that Mañjuśrī alone is capable of inquiring after the illness;
third, there are five [sections].
First is the measure for answering questions according to the occasion;
fourth, the two measures for interpreting the scriptures.
First is the intent of the initial arrival, which accords with the hearts of the assembly’s yearning and aspiration.
Second, it clarifies how the three contemplations encompass [the teachings].
Third, it swiftly accomplishes the transformation of the Tathāgata’s Pure Land.
Fourth, it serves as the skillful means for entering the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
The fifth is the seal of returning to the Buddha’s samādhi.
First, for those in the assembly who were thirsting with longing,
[Vimalakīrti] extolled the supreme wisdom and supreme virtues of the various kings, officials, commoners, disciples, and bodhisattvas.
Although the great assembly has conceived a deep longing, they have not yet been able to see or hear [the Buddha].

If one does not transmit the words and inquire after his illness on his behalf, how can we reach him? Only through this can the faithful understand the two types of illness—the provisional and the real—and awaken to the profound meaning of inconceivable liberation.
Second, the clarification of how the three contemplations encompass and lead [the practitioner] in.
Above, in the "Chapter on Expedient Means," the attachment to existence held by the king and ministers was rebuked;
in the "Chapter on Disciples," the delusion regarding emptiness held by the śrāvakas was rebuked.
In the "Bodhisattva Chapter," the expedient practices of bodhisattvas whose cultivation is not yet perfected are criticized.
Were it not for Mañjuśrī and Vimalakīrti’s dialogue and guidance,
how could one awaken to and enter the gate of perfect subtlety?

Therefore, Mañjuśrī entered and engaged in a dialogue with Vimalakīrti to proclaim the single mind and the threefold contemplation, so that they might realize the ultimate and inconceivable path of non-duality;
it is for this reason that the subsequent chapters follow.
Third, for those who would swiftly accomplish the transformation of a Tathāgata’s pure land:
if, through Mañjuśrī’s inquiry after his illness, they hear the teaching on inconceivable liberation,
they will resolve their doubts through the three contemplations and awaken to the entry into non-duality.
From the outset, one realizes that both the pure and the defiled are neither defiled nor pure;
since defilement and purity exist for the sake of sentient beings and are not true defilement or purity,
one attains the Pure Land of the Dharma-nature.
Fourth, regarding those who are the heirs of the *Mahāvaipulya* [Great Extensive] *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, there are two types:

those of the Two Vehicles who are skillful means, and bodhisattvas of sharp faculties who attain the realization of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) on that very seat. These two are distinguished by their observation of the causes of their respective faculties.
The Great Being’s voice praises the perfect and wondrous;
the Śrāvakas cry out in self-lamentation;
the Bodhisattvas’ clinging calculations gradually melt away.
Reaching the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* and the "Expedient Means" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*,
one attains the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and opens the Buddha's knowledge and vision,
eventually attaining the eternally abiding, wondrous fruit.
Fifth is the seal of returning and stabilization:
if one relies on Mañjuśrī’s exposition of the texts of the six chapters,
one extensively expounds the two aspects of the provisional and the real.
Extensively benefiting sentient beings through the true and the responsive is immediately attained;
Vimalakīrti upholds the multitude and returns them to the Perfect.
Praising and extolling, he seals and confirms the different modes of Buddha-work.

Beholding Abhirati brings about the great benefit of inconceivable liberation and the purification of the Buddha-land for the sake of benefiting sentient beings; there are many reasons why Mañjuśrī alone is capable of inquiring after the illness.
Only five types emerge.
First, they are capable because their status is high;
although Mañjuśrī and the various bodhisattvas dwell together in the stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi), [they are not so designated].
Moreover, there are degrees of depth even within the initial resolve and the subsequent stages.
Thus, the *Ratnavyūha-sūtra* states:
"Although one dwells in the stage of Equal Enlightenment..."
Abiding for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, one enters the gate of profound mystery;
this is because the initial mind of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) is shallow,
whereas Mañjuśrī and Vimalakīrti, being at the stage of the subsequent mind of Equal Enlightenment, possess a high level of realization and are thus capable [of such discourse].
Others are incapable because their status is low.
Second, regarding those who are capable because they manifest traces:
most of these people actually abide in the stage of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi).
Mañjuśrī, whose true name is Liṅzhong Jinli (Golden Grain of the Dragon Race), is in essence a being of Equal Enlightenment;
others who are merely "real" [ordinary beings] cannot [endure this],
whereas Mañjuśrī can, as he is likewise a manifested trace.
Third, regarding the manifestation of perfection:
how could the original and manifested traces of the Great Beings be definitively measured?
However, because these Bodhisattvas assist the Buddha by frequently manifesting gates of expedient teaching, they were all refuted by Vimalakīrti.
Mañjuśrī, as the Pure Name (Vimalakīrti), assists the Buddha to manifest the Perfect [Teaching].
Since that which is manifested is identical [to that of the other bodhisattvas], he alone is capable [of this task].
Fourth, the various bodhisattvas who assist the Buddha in his activities satisfy the sentiments of sentient beings.
Why is it that you do not expound the Perfect [Teaching] at all?
It is simply because the conditions for transforming sentient beings are shallow; even if I were to go and inquire after your illness, [it would be of no avail].
The sentiments of the multitude were not yet satisfied.
Mañjuśrī’s conditions for transforming sentient beings were profound;
if you go to inquire, he will surely be joyful and comforted, and only you are capable of this alone.
Fifth, their capacities and conditions differ.
The various bodhisattvas and Vimalakīrti possess the capacity for both refutation and guidance,
like a mortar and pestle shaping objects.
Mañjuśrī and Vimalakīrti engaged in a dynamic interaction like two hammers striking together to form an object; thus,
as Mañjuśrī entered the room, they alternately served as host and guest, mutually responding and completing one another.
Furthermore, he accomplishes the benefit of sentient beings, bringing great advantage to those aided.
Regarding the illness inquired about by the Three Knowledges (Traividyā),
there are two kinds.
The first is the actual illness,
which has outflowing karma as its cause;
the second is the expedient illness.
Arisen from great compassion,
the Pure Name (Vimalakīrti) was able to manifest illness where there was no illness; therefore,
this is called "expedient means" (upāya).
The delusions and karma that give rise to sentient beings are what constitute the "real.
Therefore, the subsequent passage states that the bodhisattva’s illness arises from great compassion;
this is precisely the "expedient" (upāya).
"Now, these pains of mine all arise from the delusions and afflictions of inverted false perceptions in past lives;
this is the reality.
To explain these two ailments constitutes two gates.
The former is the reality and the latter is the expedient means.
To explain the reality, I shall briefly set forth three sections.
The first is the differentiation of cause and effect.
Second, the mutual intermingling of cause and effect;
third, the relative nature of light and heavy [offenses].
First, regarding the distinction between cause and effect:
The three causes are precisely the karma and its fruits produced by these four afflictions—greed, hatred, delusion, and their equal parts.
Therefore, a sutra says:
"All arise from the afflictions of false appearances and inversions in previous lives."
Furthermore, the Great Sūtra states:
"Greed, hatred, delusion, and pride constitute the causes of suffering.
As for what is called the "suffering of the resultant characteristic":

From those causes of outflow (āsrava), one brings about as a result a body composed of the four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—and the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging (pañcopādānaskandha) characterized by birth, old age, sickness, and death.
As for their correspondences: greed corresponds to the water element.
The Sūtra says:
"From water, craving arises;
second, hatred corresponds to the fire element."
The Sūtra says:
"Hatred burns away the roots of goodness.
The three types of delusion correspond to the element of wind.
The Sūtra states:
"The violent winds of the four inversions correspond to the earth element of the four equal parts;
these equal parts are identical in nature to the simultaneous arising of the three poisons."
The earth element, as well as the other three great elements, must necessarily coexist.
Furthermore, the *Sūtra of Auspicious Responses* states:
"Greed and desire lead to old age."
Hatred causes illness; delusion causes death.
By inferring from this principle, one may understand the arising of the "equal-parts" (sāmagrī) temperament.
Therefore, the subsequent text states:
"Where there is birth and death, there is illness.
As for the second point, the mutual entanglement of cause and effect:
When greed and hatred arise alternately among the six sense organs and their myriad objects, there are eighty-four thousand afflictions; this is the disease.
When the four elements each arise and mutually clash and rub against one another, [the same occurs].
The one great disharmony results in the hundred and one afflictions of disease;
the four hundred and four diseases extend even to the fruit of ten thousand maladies and pestilence.
Third, regarding the relative nature of light and heavy [suffering]:
If one follows the ordinary three poisons while concurrently practicing the precepts of taking refuge,
it is called "light. If one commits the ten evil deeds,
the four grave offenses, the five heinous crimes, severs the roots of goodness, or slanders the Dharma, this is called "increased gravity."
Light causes result in the retribution of the four great elements and the four sufferings within the realms of humans and devas;
this is called the "light fruit.
As for the three miserable paths and the Avīci Hell, these are places where the four great elements and the four sufferings are intensified.
This refers to the importance of the fruit.
Second, regarding the clarification of provisional illness:
the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* elucidates the five practices.

These are called the noble conduct (*ārya-caryā*), the celestial conduct (*divya-caryā*), the Brahma conduct (*brahma-caryā*), the infantile conduct (*bāla-caryā*), and the sickly conduct (*glāna-caryā*).
Of these five types of conduct, the first three are for one's own benefit, while the latter two are for the benefit of others.
Thus, those that accord with the side of minor virtues are termed "infantile conduct."
That which is on the side of the afflictions is called the practice of illness;
great loving-kindness gives rise to the practice of an infant,
and great compassion gives rise to the practice of illness.
Therefore, the subsequent passage states:
"The illness of the Bodhisattva arises next because it is preceded by great compassion.
As the Mahāyāna Sūtra says:
When a bodhisattva abides in the Samādhi of the Three Truths,
they possess twenty-five samādhis,
which cure the ailments of sentient beings within the twenty-five states of existence.
Regarding the twenty-fifth, there are those who possess samādhis.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra states:
"First, the stainless samādhi (vimala-samādhi) destroys the existence of the hells."
The *Avivartya-samādhi* destroys existence as an animal;
the *Cittaratā-samādhi* destroys existence as a hungry ghost;
the *Prāmodya-samādhi* destroys existence as an asura.
The Illusion-like Samādhi destroys existence in Jambudvīpa;
the Sunlight Samādhi destroys existence in Pūrvavideha;
the Moonlight Samādhi destroys existence in Aparagoyānī.
The Samādhi of the Blazing Flame destroys existence in the northern direction;
the Samādhi of Immovability destroys existence among the Four Heavenly Kings;
the Samādhi of the Unconquerable destroys existence among the Trāyastriṃśa gods.
The Samādhi of Delighting the Multitudes destroys existence in Yama;
the Blue Samādhi destroys existence in Tuṣita;
the Yellow Samādhi destroys existence in Nirmāṇarati.
The red-colored samādhi destroys the existence of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven;
the white-colored samādhi destroys the existence of the First Dhyāna;
and the variegated samādhi destroys the existence of the Brahmā King.
The Samādhi of the Pair breaks the existence of the second dhyāna;
the Samādhi of Thunderous Sound breaks the existence of the third dhyāna;
the Samādhi of Pouring Rain breaks the existence of the fourth dhyāna.
The Samādhi of Non-obstruction destroys the existence of non-conceptualization;
the Samādhi of the Illuminating Mirror destroys the existence of the intermediate state (*nāmakāya*);
and the Samādhi Like Space destroys the existence of the sphere of infinite space.
The samādhi of permanence destroys existence in the sphere of infinite consciousness;
the samādhi of bliss destroys existence in the sphere of nothingness;
the samādhi of self destroys existence in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Fourth, I shall provide a comprehensive explanation of this chapter and the following five chapters by means of both the provisional and the ultimate [teachings].
Regarding what applies to this chapter:

it begins from the passage, "Householder, from what cause does this illness arise? and extends down to, "The illnesses of sentient beings arise from the four great elements; because they have illness, I too have illness."
The clarity and purity of the name "Great Compassion" refers to the skillful means of manifesting illness to benefit sentient beings;
from "consoling sentient beings" downward,
it describes the consolation provided through external matters after they have been tamed.
Internal contemplation and subduing constitute the actual object of transformation;
the text contains three points of urgency,
namely, subduing.
In the beginning of the text, first, one uses emptiness (*śūnyatā*) to regulate attachment to existence;
second, from "by means of that which has nothing to receive, one receives all sensations" onwards,
one enters into the conventional through great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) to regulate the illness of emptiness through existence.
From "The three are neither true nor existent" onwards,
one employs the practice of what has not yet been heard;
this is the first emptiness, which quickly eliminates the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) by deconstructing existence.
Second, by means of the wondrous existence that is entirely empty, one overcomes the disease of countless forms of ignorance;
third, by means of the correct contemplation of the Middle Way, one eliminates the disease of the dwelling-place of ignorance.
This applies throughout the following five sections of the sutra text.
In the "Chapter on Inquiring after Illness," he briefly inquired about the two types of illness—
the provisional and the real. Eight thousand devaputras of slight defilement gave rise to the bodhicitta,
while the other great beings (mahāsattvas) did not yet do so.
Therefore, in the five chapters following the "Vimalakīrti" and "Mañjuśrī," the two types of illness are explained in detail.
Specifically, in the "Inconceivable" chapter, the great provisional and skillful application of the Bodhisattva is expounded;
this is called the "Extensive Provisional Illness."
The "Chapter on Observing Sentient Beings" extensively clarifies emptiness (*śūnyatā*);
the "Chapter on the Buddha-Way" extensively clarifies the provisional (*prajñapti*);
and the "Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of Nonduality" and the "Chapter on the Fragrant Accumulation" extensively clarify the Middle Way and the ultimate reality. These are swift [in their realization].
The principles of these words are vast and expansive, containing many parables;
