the realization of the Way and the attainment of its fruits therein bring great benefit.
Thus we know that although the six chapters of the sutra differ in their phrasing and expressions, their underlying meaning is consistent and their principles accord with one another.
This always clarifies the bodhisattva’s practice of illness.
Mañjuśrī is here translated as Miaode (Wondrous Virtue);
in the new [translation], he is called Miaojixiang (Wondrous Auspiciousness).
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, Part Two, nurtures this [teaching].
Those who have already been transformed by the Buddha and whose names are inscribed upon the highest and most honored [register]— those whose sentiments reach deep—
are said to praise the supreme purity of the Name (Vimalakīrti).
It is called "profound" because it causes those who go together as a community to give rise to deep faith and sincerity.
"The empty room" symbolizes the vast principle of the Pure Land. Within the canopy, Śākyamuni’s manifestation of the Buddha-land while preaching the Dharma represents this very point.
Vimalakīrti demonstrated that he did not deviate from the fundamental principle;
his empty room manifested the significance of the "fangzhang" (the master’s quarters).
Thus, Mañjuśrī asked why the room was empty.
Therefore, the answer was given:
"The lands of all Buddhas are likewise entirely empty. Furthermore, because sentient beings were formerly deluded, the Pure Land transformed into the triple world;
the Dharma-body transformed into celestial demons and external paths.
The compassionate transformation of Vimalakīrti was likewise not manifest;
now, as Mañjuśrī enters the room for discussion,
the multitude of sentient beings will surely attain awakening.
Upon awakening, one realizes that the nature of the triple world is empty;
thus, an empty room symbolizes this.
Because attachment and views have returned to the Way, there is no attendant.
This manifests the compassionate vows of Vimalakīrti.
Thus, in manifesting his deliverance, he comes with the aspect of not coming.
Zhiyi said:
Dharma Master Kumārajīva rectified the profound essence and extracted the hidden meaning of the texts.

Only then did he realize that previous translations had injured the original and that their phrasing deviated from the intended purport. For instance, [the former versions] took the "mark of non-coming" as "bringing disgrace," the "mark of non-seeing" as "seeing," the "unconditioned dharma" as "the initial spirit," and "conditioned harmony" as "the cessation of the mind."
There is no category that does not include such cases;
the Dharma Master has corrected them all accordingly.
Furthermore, it is because he was originally at the Āmra Grove that he did not come [previously], but now comes.
Because he sees an empty room, he sees by not seeing.
Furthermore, because hundreds of thousands of devas and humans are obstructed by existence (*bhava*), they definitely see the five hundred śrāvakas;
because he speaks of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), he does not see the bodhisattvas.
Because it abides in the middle, one sees by not seeing.
Furthermore, because sentient beings are deluded regarding birth, they see [birth] coming;
because they are deluded regarding death, they see [death] going.
Furthermore, within the cycle of birth and death, one cannot avoid coming and going;
it is only by means of the Great Being’s coming and going in response to sentient beings that one finally realizes there is ultimately no coming or going.
Furthermore, seeing the principle of signlessness is called "truly not seeing.
Grasping at the signs of the six sense objects is not true seeing.
Since time immemorial, sentient beings have been falsely attached to these counterfeit views.
Now, when Mañjuśrī enters the chamber, he will surely cause sentient beings to see the signless; this seeing of the signless is what can truly be seen.
As for seeing through deluded signs and inverted views, these will naturally persist without interruption and can no longer be seen [as true].
Regarding whether it can be endured or not:
since the Bodhisattva himself is free from illness,
how could there be anything that is either endurable or unendurable?
Since it is for the sake of the illnesses of sentient beings,
then the illness of sentient beings may be endured,
and the illness of the bodhisattva may be endured.
The illnesses of sentient beings are unbearable;
the Bodhisattva’s [compassion] is likewise unbearable.
If one discusses illness with respect to sentient beings to distinguish between what is bearable and what is unbearable:
Not falling into the eight difficult conditions and being born to encounter the Buddha-dharma is called "endurance.
Hearing the Dharma and practicing it accordingly is called "healing with reduction.
Receiving it once and never regressing is called "increase."
Furthermore, the five heinous crimes, the severing of roots of goodness, and the slandering of the Vaipulya sutras cannot be expiated through repentance; these are "unbearable" (akṣānti).
Other offenses are "bearable" (kṣānti) because they do not belong to the category of those fixed in wrongness (mithyātva-niyata-rāśi). This is also acceptable.
All transgressions mentioned previously lead to rebirth in the three evil realms and are thus intolerable.
Because one has already taken the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts and knows that cultivating roots of goodness is superior, these [transgressions] may be tolerated.
Furthermore, the cycle of saṃsāra within the three realms is entirely intolerable.
The renunciation of the two vehicles may be tolerated.
Furthermore, that the two vehicles—being of the "half-syllable" (ardha-akṣara) type—are stalled at that "transformed city" (nirmita-nagara) cannot be tolerated;
only the Mahāyāna of the "full-syllable" (pūrṇa-akṣara) is truly called tolerable.
Furthermore, the provisional Mahāyāna that has not yet entered the perfect and subtle is called "unbearable";
only the ultimate, sudden, and perfect [teaching] is called "bearable.
This serves to treat and heal those who have been impaired.
This also concerns whether a bodhisattva causes harm or no harm to sentient beings.
A Mahāsattva treats sentient beings with the medicine of the Dharma; whether this results in harm or no harm should be analyzed through four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
A single root of dullness obstructs the heavy;
the power of the roots of goodness is feeble,
and one is driven by heavy karma.
The administration of the medicine of the Dharma cannot be impaired by two factors: dullness of faculties and being hindered by light [obstacles].
For example, the bhikṣu Paṇḍita recited a single verse and attained the fruit of Arhatship.
Three factors—sharpness of faculties and being hindered by heavy [obstacles]—are [the opposite].
For example, Aṅgulimāla, who had killed people, attained awakening upon seeing the Buddha;
those with sharp faculties are exempt from being disparaged.
Likewise, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana attained the Way upon hearing the Two Truths.
Kāśyapa, by their very nature, these [beings] do not possess such qualities.
Regarding these four types: the first does not suffer diminution when entering meditative absorption for the first time;

the second and third suffer diminution due to surpassing the Buddha’s superior conditions, yet they do not suffer diminution if they do not surpass those superior conditions; as for the fourth person, he suffers diminution in all cases and does not reach increase.
This also distinguishes between increase and non-increase by means of whether the illnesses of sentient beings increase or do not increase.
For example, there are four types of illness among worldly people.
The first is that which gradually increases from the time one contracts the illness; this is called "increasing increase."
2. When the initial [offense] is grave and the subsequent one is more so, it is called "increasing" (vṛddhi).

3. When the initial [offense] is diminished and the subsequent one increases, it is called "diminishing" (hāni). 4. When the initial [offense] is light and the subsequent one is diminished, it is called "diminishing the diminishing" (hānihāni).
Based on this, it is clarified that there are also four types of bodhisattvas who deliver sentient beings.
The first is "increasing the increasing," such as those like Sunakṣatra and Devadatta, who are of the class that destroys the Dharma and disrupts the Saṃgha.
Regarding the second case, where there is an increase at the beginning and a decrease at the end:
this refers to those such as Aṅgulimāla,
whose initial karma of killing and so forth was extremely grave.
Later, having left the household life and heard the Dharma, his awakening was even more profound.
Third, regarding that which initially decreases but later increases,
this is as explained in the *Śāstra*.
A certain bhikṣu cultivated and attained the four dhyānas, taking them to be the four fruits of the path.
At the time of his death, he saw his place of rebirth and consequently slandered [the existence of] nirvāṇa.
They will consequently fall into hell.
This also applies to those who have left the household life for the sake of the Dharma but subsequently become mired in fame and profit, or who cling to their teachers while slandering the Dharma;
such individuals are said to "diminish and increase" [the truth].

Regarding the "four types of those who cause harm," these refer to the noble ones such as Śāriputra and others. As for the phrase "from delusion there is craving," there is an interpretation by a master [as follows]:
Delusion is the confusion regarding principles through false views;
craving is the confusion regarding phenomena through greed and hatred.
These two afflictions encompass all afflictions.
The various ailments of birth and death arise from this.
It is further said:
delusion is the past cause of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Craving and views are the present causes that project this current body;
they project a future body as well.
Because this continuity of delusion and craving causes the wheel of the twelve links of dependent origination to revolve without ceasing, it is called "arising from birth.
This clarifies that the beginning of compassion need not be described solely in terms of what has already been accomplished.
Compassion based on conditions arises from the initial resolve;
compassion that is objectless is of the same essence as the bodies of all Buddhas.
This means that the ignorance and craving of sentient beings share the same source as the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
The objectless great compassion is of one essence with True Suchness.
When sentient beings first turn their backs on the Dharma-nature, it is called ignorance and craving;
when Bodhisattvas reverse delusion and realize this nature, it is called great compassion.
Therefore, what is said here refers to the essence of compassion itself, rather than being designated by way of the arousal of the resolve [for awakening].
As for the "sixty-two views," they are called "views" because they arise in opposition to the principle.
Regarding the "sixty-two," the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* states in the verse of the chapter on Nirvāṇa:
Whether existence or non-existence after cessation,
finitude and so forth, permanence and so forth—
all such views depend upon nirvāṇa.
The future is also the past.
The commentary states:
"Regarding whether [the Buddha] exists or does not exist after cessation," and so forth.
That is to say: whether the Tathāgata exists after his parinirvāṇa, or whether the Tathāgata does not exist,
or whether he both exists and does not exist,
or whether he neither exists nor does not exist.
These four views arise based on nirvāṇa:
that the self and the world are finite, infinite, both, or neither.
These four views arise based on the future life.
The four views—such as whether the self and the world are eternal, non-eternal, both, or neither—arise based on the past life.
When these twelve views are applied across the five aggregates, they result in sixty views, as set forth in the verse.
It further says:
"What is this 'one fruit'?
The prose commentary explains:

What is the view that the body is identical to the self? This is the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*). What is the view that the body is different from the self? This is the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*). Based upon these sixty views, one adds these two fundamental views of annihilationism and eternalism, which results in the sixty-two views. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, in the "Mother of Buddhas" chapter, states: "That the self and the world are eternal—this is the truth, all else is false speech... and so on, up to: "That the self and the world are finite, infinite, both, or neither—all such attachments to views are called the sixty-two views."
Question: Why is it that being free from the sixty-two views is itself the liberation of all Buddhas? Answer:
The treatise verse states:
"The limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) of nirvāṇa and the limit of the world—between these twelve limits, there is not the slightest difference.
The treatise further states in verse:
All phenomena cannot be extinguished;
all conceptual proliferations are without person and without location.
Even the Buddha has nothing to discourse upon.
The equality of the two limits and the departure from all conceptual proliferation is called the liberation of the Dharma-Buddha. All Māras and externalists are my attendants;
"Māra" refers to those attached to craving and delusion.
The non-Buddhists cling to views as delusion;
the provisional teaching explains that the overcoming of craving constitutes meditative concentration,
while the destruction of views constitutes wisdom.
This concentration accords with the true name and is thus called "with attendant.
In the present Perfect and Subtle Teaching,
one awakens to the fact that attachment itself is liberation.
To fully comprehend false views is itself right view.
Since bondage and liberation are equal and the false and the correct are non-dual, there is no one to attend upon. Regarding "consoling and encouraging," etc.:
Fearing that newly initiated bodhisattvas might become terrified of birth and death and thereby regress from their great compassion, he consoles them;
for if they realize that conditioned phenomena are impermanent, suffering,
and so forth, they will no longer crave the world.
Neither craving the world nor clinging to the world,
one is then able to extensively accumulate merit and wisdom.
Once merit and wisdom have been accumulated,
birth and death naturally cannot cause affliction.
If one is able to not fear birth and death, [then one is truly liberated].
The practice of great compassion is thereby perfected.
Furthermore, because one has [transcended] the burden of karmic offenses, one does not fear birth and death;
this is called being able to give rise to the bodhicitta in a single thought-moment.
If one rejoices in the Mahāyāna for even a single thought-moment, all transgressions will naturally perish;
what, then, is there to fear?
Thus, the Ratnakūṭa Sūtra says:
The moment one gives rise to the bodhicitta, all transgressions are extinguished.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Upon hearing the two characters for 'eternal abiding,' one shall not fall into the evil realms."
Those who hear the Lotus Sutra with pure faith will always be born in the presence of the Buddhas.
Furthermore, because they pity those who have received bodies not bound by their own karma, they remain free from worldly entanglements.
Moreover, they avoid the fruitless births they would have otherwise endured throughout long kalpas of past lives.
Since one cannot [avoid] this now, what cause for concern is there in answering sentient beings?
Furthermore, when compassion gives rise to love, merit increases immeasurably.
When merit has accumulated and its retribution is supreme, what fear could there be?
Furthermore, since the principle is thus, one abides in peace without anxiety; this absence of anxiety is the Way, specifically termed "advancing on the Way."
One immediately becomes a King of Physicians;
once this fruit is realized, one is able to universally succor all classes of beings.
Such is my aspiration.
Therefore, it is said that the Buddha spoke provisionally of the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and bases (āyatanas).
Now one knows that within these phenomena such as the aggregates, there is truly no self.
Having eliminated the view of a self, one attains the fruits of the Two Vehicles.
Although the two vehicles have eliminated the view of a self,
they do not understand that the Tathāgata’s provisional teaching on the aggregates and elements is a conceptual construct; to grasp these as real is called attachment to phenomena (dharmagrāha).

Therefore, the Buddha next taught the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), and bases of consciousness (āyatana) within the Mahāyāna, explaining that their arising is without intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva),
so as to lead beings to realize the contemplation of the dharma of non-arising and non-ceasing.
These are precisely the three categories— aggregates, bases, and elements— in which the grasping at a self (ātma-grāha) occurs.
By means of the three types of conventional designations—causal, continuous, and relative—the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) is simultaneously sublated.
The sickness of emptiness likewise precedes the two sicknesses of self and phenomena;
to grasp at phenomena as being substantially existent is itself a sickness.
To realize that all phenomena are fundamentally illusory is to eliminate the disease.
Now, this third ailment—clinging to emptiness—is the attachment to a "non-existence" that results from abandoning existence; it becomes a disease because of such verbal fixation.
If one realizes that words are provisional, the disease will naturally vanish.
Therefore, it is said:
"For now, eliminate them by means of verbal traces;
these are merely verbal traces."
It appears to exist, yet it is not said to be real.
Furthermore, the Buddha designates emptiness by way of conventional names in order to eliminate the notion of "existence" held by ordinary beings who believe things are definitively existent.
Thus, existence is neither existent nor non-existent,
and emptiness is likewise neither empty nor non-empty;
yet those who are deluded, upon hearing of emptiness, are unable to relinquish their attachment to existence.
Consequently, one abandons existence and clings to emptiness;
thus it is said: "Emptiness is itself a sickness, for it is because of the sickness of existence that there is emptiness."
This means that existence itself is emptiness.
This emptiness is free from affliction;
it is only when one abandons existence and clings to emptiness that having emptiness becomes an affliction.
Therefore, the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra says:
"All teachings regarding emptiness are intended to destroy all forms of existence.
If there were anyone who could grasp emptiness," [it would not be so].
The Buddhas do not perform such acts.
Master Zhaò also said:
"To abandon existence and go toward emptiness."
It is like fleeing from a mountain peak only to rush into an abyss;
both fail to avoid calamity. Because he does not undergo any further sensations, this is the Great Being’s great compassion entering into conventional reality to transform sentient beings.
This refers to the second stage in the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* (Yíngluò jīng), which involves entering the contemplation from emptiness into the provisional.
Previously, the virtues of the Bodhisattva were praised, stating that he opens and closes the gates of all evil destinies,
yet manifests his body within the five realms of existence.
In the "Expedient Means" chapter, Vimalakīrti dwells in brothels and wine shops;
furthermore, in the subsequent "Buddha Path" chapter, it is clarified that practicing what is not the path constitutes the Buddha path.
All of these are instances of the Bodhisattva’s correct awakening to non-arising (*anutpāda*).
He contemplates the three realms, the six paths, and the nirvana of the two vehicles as being like dreams, illusions, bubbles, and foam;
thus, there is no karma to be experienced. Out of great compassion, he manifests provisional traces and takes birth through shared activity.
Therefore, it is said that they "receive" [it].
Since what is received by those in the three realms and six paths, as well as by the two vehicles and those in nirvana, is not the same,
it is thus stated.
Regarding the statement, "Attachment to the savor of meditative absorption (dhyāna-rasa) among all feelings is a bond for the bodhisattva," the commentary states:
This refers to the birth in the higher realms and the attainment of realization by those of the Two Vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha).
All of this arises from being attached to dhyāna.
Furthermore, it is explained that the flavor of dhyāna in the higher realms is subsumed under the gates of craving and views.
Regarding the "taste of dhyāna" mentioned here,
it refers exclusively to the two vehicles dwelling in the samādhi of emptiness, becoming mired in emptiness and stagnating in quiescence;
for this reason, it constitutes a bondage.
Therefore, the Śrīmālā-sūtra says:
"The followers of the Two Vehicles hold the vessel of the samādhi of emptiness and are intoxicated by the wine of the signlessness of prajñā.
This is precisely what that refers to.
Regarding "born through skillful means," the commentary states:
"taking birth for the sake of sentient beings."
For that self and others are without bondage.
That which is called liberation means that following the grasping of birth constitutes bondage.
Through great wisdom, one realizes that birth is non-birth;

yet, through skillful means, one manifests birth—this skillful means is called "liberation. One who possesses the liberation of skillful means and wisdom possesses these four pillars of the two wisdoms: the provisional and the ultimate.
To possess [realization] only partially is bondage;
only by realizing the perfect can one be liberated.
It is said that in Guanzhong, those at the sixth stage and below have all realized only the partial and not yet the perfect.
From the seventh stage upward, the two types of knowledge are realized in their perfection;
it is likewise appropriate to understand it in this way.
Furthermore, according to the *Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:
From the stages of the grounds (bhūmi) upward, the two wisdoms are perfected;
from the eighth ground onward, they are employed while remaining eternally quiescent.
Thus, prior to the grounds, they constitute bondage.
Ascending the stages constitutes the explanation.

Furthermore, among these four chapters, the first two clarify skillful means with respect to the practice of transforming others, while the latter two clarify skillful means with respect to one's own practice. "Though delighting in seclusion, not relying on the exhaustion of body and mind" means:
This means that when the followers of the Two Vehicles attain extinction (*nirvāṇa*) and burn their bodies with transformative fire, it is called "exhaustion.
When they realize emptiness through the wisdom of cessation, it is called the "exhaustion of the mind.
The Dharma-body of the Bodhisattva is bodiless, yet its body is identical to those of the six realms of existence.
The true mind is without mind; yet, being without mind, its wisdom pervades all things.

Therefore, it is said to be inexhaustible. Although it acts within the three realms, it does not destroy the dharma-nature, for the three realms arise through conditions and, though they arise, they lack substantial reality.
This is precisely the *dharmatā*.
Yet, those who are deluded undergo birth within the six realms of existence, becoming defiled by and attached to their forms.
Through attachment to form, they lose the benefit [of the Dharma] and claim that the *dharmatā* is destroyed.

The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are as previously described in the "Chapter on Buddha-lands. Regarding the practice of the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) to be born in the Brahma-world without attachment:
ordinary beings rely upon the fundamental concentrations (*mauladhyāna*) and further cultivate the immeasurables to become kings among the various dhyānas.
Because the bodhisattva knows that all things are like illusions, he does not give rise to attachment. Regarding those who practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and liberation (*vimokṣa*):

meditative concentration refers to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), while the four types of concentrative absorption refer to the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) of the sphere of infinite space and so forth.
Samādhi does not refer to emptiness (śūnyatā), signlessness (animitta), or wishlessness (apraṇihita); rather,
it refers to the three samādhis characterized by applied thought (vitarka) and sustained thought (vicāra),
namely, the first dhyāna with applied and sustained thought.
The intermediate dhyāna is without vitarka but with vicāra;
from the second dhyāna onwards, there is neither vitarka nor vicāra.
These three samādhis are those through which ordinary beings take birth according to their respective dhyānas.
They are not Bodhisattvas.

If the principles of the three contemplations— emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness— and the four noble truths were not dharmas for taking birth, then they would not be the same [as the case at hand].
In the "Chapter on the Inconceivable," it says: "I have come for the sake of the Dharma, not for the sake of a bed or seat.
If Śāriputra’s thought is as follows:
"I originally came from the Āmra Grove for the sake of the Dharma."
It is not for the purpose of a bed or a seat, yet one suddenly thinks of a bed therein;
this is not the original mind. It is that which does not possess form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
This passage indicates that Vimalakīrti does not claim that because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is non-arising, there are no phenomena to be sought.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, having received his command, was followed by five hundred and eighty thousand who followed him for the sake of the Dharma.
However, since the sentiment of delighting in the Dharma is fervent,
the mind that clings to it is likewise firm;
and once the sentiment is fervent and the attachment is firm, [the result follows].
Although the three contemplations were briefly elucidated in the preceding chapter,
the Prince was merely able to resolve his mind toward awakening and had not yet attained a profound realization of the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Now, by means of the recollection of the seat, the great function of the "Inconceivable" chapter is about to be revealed.
Therefore, first dispatch the mind that stagnates in the Dharma and forget the intent to seek and grasp.
All those who come and follow will naturally find their opportunities for attachment extinguished;
they will not be left behind or lost in stagnation.
Nearby, one immediately attains the purity of the Dharma-eye;
in the distant sense, one is able to enter the gate of non-duality.

The enumeration of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*) is as extensive as the "Grove of Illumination" (*Ming-yuan*). There are none who seek through the vision of suffering.
The Four Noble Truths are of two kinds.
In the Hīnayāna, they are defined as the seeing of suffering, the abandoning of its origin, the realizing of its cessation, and the practicing of the path;
herein, this suffering is the actual suffering that constitutes the profound truth.
The same applies up to the cessation and the path.
In the Mahāyāna, the realization that suffering is non-arising is called "suffering.
This is true for the truths up to the origin and cessation as well.
These Four Truths are in fact the One True Truth.
Although they are designated as four, their essence is one;
this differs from the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna), where both the designation and the essence are fourfold.
Sida replied: "To know that suffering is non-arising is called the Truth of Suffering;
to know that the origin is without conjunction is called the Noble Truth of the Origin."
To contemplate through the mark of non-duality is called the Noble Truth of the Path.
That phenomena are fundamentally unborn and thus now do not cease is called the Noble Truth of Cessation.
This is the Four Noble Truths of Non-arising in the Mahāyāna.
If the *Śālistamba Sūtra* (The Sutra of the Buddha’s Bequeathed Teaching) says:
"The Buddha taught that the Truth of Suffering is truly suffering."
It must not be made otherwise.
That "the collection of reality is the cause" and so forth refers precisely to the Four Noble Truths of the Hīnayāna.
Furthermore, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states:

"Ordinary beings possess suffering but lack the [noble] truth, for they give rise to the notion of pleasure; the followers of the Two Vehicles possess both suffering and the truth, for they realize the suffering of the aggregates; the Bodhisattvas understand that suffering is non-suffering yet possess the true truth, for they realize the non-arising of the aggregates. Thus, it is said in the *Kātyāyanāvavāda*:
The five aggregates wither away, reaching emptiness where nothing arises; this is the meaning of suffering (*duḥkha*).
This, too, is awakening to the non-arising of suffering, which is called the meaning of suffering. Furthermore, the text below states:

"Based on the meaning of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, one clearly proclaims impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self. This, too, is the realization that suffering has no master, which is called true reality. Regarding what was cited above concerning the non-arising of suffering and so forth:
This means there is no seeking to see suffering, nor even no seeking to abandon the origin [of suffering],
and so forth. If one says, "I shall see suffering, abandon the origin, realize cessation, and cultivate the path," this is already a failure to understand arising.
This deviates from the true nature of reality;
it is not genuine discourse, but is called frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*). As for *yojana*: [it is a unit of distance].
Some call it *yojana*, some call it *yuzhen* (由延), and some call it *youxun yushanjna* (俞旬踰繕那).
According to the phonetic reconstruction, it should be as follows.
This means that it is calculated and measured to be so;
it is equivalent to one *fangyi* (a Chinese postal station) in this region.
According to the ancient sage-kings, one day’s journey was sixteen *li* of *krośas*.
In other sutras and treatises, the number is sometimes thirty-six, eighteen, or ten;
there is no fixed number.
This is seen in Master Ying’s *Jingyin* (Phonetics of the Sutra). Regarding the statement, "This seat is so high and broad that I cannot ascend it":

In the past, at the Deer Park, the Tathāgata taught the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) concerning the four truths of arising and ceasing and the twelve links of dependent origination, thereby severing the delusions of the nine stages within the three realms.
He proceeded until, upon the ninth bed of liberation—the stage of non-characteristic perception—he realized the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising.
This is called "sitting upon the bed of liberation.
When the Tathāgata received and guided those of the two vehicles, he said:
"I and you three persons sit together upon the bed of liberation."
These śrāvakas and others do not understand the true principle of the Tathāgata’s teaching according to his expedient means—that the Tathāgata sits together with them upon this bed of liberation.
Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says:
"The Buddha speaks of the single meaning of liberation," yet they are unable to attain this Dharma.
Since the followers of the Two Vehicles claim that they sit together with the Buddha,
how could they possibly strive for further progress?
Now, I intend to take away their understanding of liberation so that they may know it is not the true seat.
Now, one realizes the true seat of inconceivable liberation;
yet, since principle cannot be realized instantaneously, there must necessarily be a gradual process.
Therefore, by provisionally employing the throne of the Lamp-King (Dīpaṃkara), the provisional is dispatched so as to reach the ultimate reality.
Therefore, the Lotus Sūtra says:
"If you merely distance yourselves from falsehood, it is called liberation;
yet in reality, you have not attained all-encompassing liberation."
Why is it compared to a bed? Answer:
Because liberation is rest, the Tathāgata is the bed. There are those who possess supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) but do not possess the inconceivable (*acintya*).
The supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) of the two vehicles increase in the small and decrease in the great.
Since they have not yet realized that the essence of the small and the great is one,
they maintain that things possess fixed characteristics of being either large or small.
The manifestation of these powers functions by increasing or decreasing their magnitude;
because there is this process of increase and decrease,
one perceives the distinct forms of large and small.
Therefore, it is called "beyond thought and speculation.

The Bodhisattva knows that the Middle Way exhausts all extremes; through provisional contemplation, the true, perfect, and wondrous principle manifests, wherein the forms of the Great and Small Vehicles and the functions of wisdom are darkly merged within the wondrous essence.
It is like a bright mirror that has no mind of its own, yet clearly distinguishes between the beautiful and the ugly.
Truly, without exertion, life spans naturally shift;
this is the innate supernatural power of the Dharmakāya.
How could it be the supernatural power of the two vehicles, which relies on the exertion of effort and the application of the mind in their initial meditative concentrations?
Question:
What is the difference between the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of the two vehicles, which are attained through mental cultivation, and the innate supernormal powers of a bodhisattva? Answer:
There is a vast difference.

The followers of the Two Vehicles manifest supernatural powers by relying on the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) upon their own minds, which have been acquired as a result of conditioned existence;
as soon as the mind moves, [the power] is present.
When the mind perishes, it is non-existent.
The Bodhisattva awakens to and penetrates the essence and function of the dharma-nature, achieving its full perfection.
While the essence of the dharma-nature is eternally constant, its function gives rise to birth and extinction.
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) inherently possesses function; how could it be something produced through cultivation?
Furthermore, it is used constantly through its quiescence.
To function while remaining constantly quiescent is the principle.
There is no function apart from its essence,
nor is there an essence apart from its function;
since it is such that essence and function are identical, [they are inseparable].
How could there be any intentional application of the mind?
This is the penetration of the Bodhisattva’s dharma-nature;
how could it be the penetration of the meditative power of the two vehicles? Why is it that we have forever severed our roots?
Formerly, I heard that what is called "according with suitability" is identical to the Buddha’s seat of liberation.
Now I hear there is another liberation called "inconceivable," which,
when measured, proves that external practices are not its equal.
I have also scrutinized that internal realization is not ultimate reality.
Furthermore, the practices of a Mahāsattva require more than three asaṃkhyeya kalpas to complete;
I have now severed the fetters.
His life was exceedingly short, and as there was no further stage for his cultivation,
he has brought about this grief of eternal severance.
Furthermore, I have examined that what he realized was not the same as that of the Buddha.
This refers to the teaching that curdles milk into fresh butter (*navanīta*); the first two fruits of the *Avataṃsaka* vehicle, being as yet unsubstantial, are called "milk.
Just as the *Āgamas* transform the ordinary into the noble by transforming milk into curd.
Formerly, I held that the three vehicles equally realize the ninth liberation;
now I know that the Buddha’s teaching is not the same.

from the Brahmakāyika and Brahmapurohita heavens, fear is born, and the Brahmā kings of the second dhyāna are the last to be reborn.
At that time, it is called the destruction of the kalpa.
After twelve eons of emptiness have passed, wind gradually arises within the realm;
as the kalpa of devas and humans is about to begin, a great wind subsequently rises,
its breadth being immeasurable multiples greater than before, and its thickness sixteen lakṣas.
Indestructible even by vajras, this is named the Wind of the Realm-Sustaining Radiant Sound Golden Treasury Wheel.
It fills the three thousandfold world-system like rain from a pivot;
the wind obstructs it, not allowing it to flow away.
The wind blows and forms ice that freezes,
first creating a vajra-wheel four hundred yojanas in extent; next,
vajra-clouds pour down rain to fill its interior, first forming the realm of Brahmā.
In succession, one reaches the four heavens; according to the stages of sentient beings' formation, there is Mount Sumeru, the seven mountain ranges, and so forth;
to the north, west, east, and south are the realms of hungry ghosts and animals, extending even to the hell realms.
When one cycle of increase and decrease has passed, it is then called the establishment of the receptacle world.
Those whose merit in the second dhyāna is exhausted are not reborn in Jambudvīpa;
their physical stature is already doubled, and what they consume is solely the essence of the earth.
When the flavor vanished, the food rose up as dew; when the dew disappeared, the food became non-glutinous rice.

Because of greed for bodily radiance, that light vanished, and from this, the sun and moon were born.

The establishment of rulers, pride, physicians, and the placement of the sick; From these, the sin of killing originated.

The *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* states:

these teachings all amount to two thousand one hundred [discourses].
Furthermore, by using these to counteract the four great elements and the six sense-decays, they become twenty-one thousand;

The *Sahā-samyak-nyāya* states:
"Each of the ten types of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) is already constituted by nine latent dispositions as its preliminary basis, thus forming one hundred.

those already arisen also number two thousand one hundred,
and those not yet arisen also number two thousand one hundred.
This totals four thousand two hundred.
Based on the predominance of greed, hatred, delusion, attachment to self,
and discursive thought, these five types of persons each have four thousand two hundred varieties, totaling twenty-one thousand.
Furthermore, by dividing each of the three poisons and so forth into four types of persons,
one arrives at eighty-four thousand;
these eighty-four thousand delusions are precisely the gates of worldly affliction (*kleśa*).
The remedy is itself a dharma-gate.
Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa* states:
"Some say that the measure of the aggregates of dharmas is as described in that treatise."
Alternatively, practicing according to the teachings on the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth as a remedy for false practice is called "entering the dharma-gate of all Buddha-dharmas.
Now, the ultimate principle is beyond words;
it relies upon manifold expressions to serve as instruction.
True reality is non-action;
it takes mundane affairs as the Buddha-work.
Therefore, every movement, posture, and ritual demeanor—all afflictions—are the Buddha-work.

Since anger and hatred are non-dual and purity and impurity are of one substance, those who enter this gate have no view of either self-aggrandizement or self-deprecation. As for the various kinds of earth:
It is explained that when Śākyamuni attained enlightenment, the ground consisted of sand and gravel;
when Maitreya attains enlightenment, the ground will consist of the seven treasures.
Because space is pure and free from defilement, there is no differentiation therein. As for the Buddha’s body having various forms:
Śākyamuni is sixteen feet tall, while Maitreya is two hundred and fifty chi; yet their unimpeded wisdom is not manifold, for they are identical in the wisdom of non-arising.
These are all views that cling to phenomena, characteristic of the Hīnayāna.
This is not the vision of one who has attained the principles of the Mahāyāna;
therefore, the Great Being (Mahāsattva) cites equality to refute it.
Furthermore, previously, when they followed Mañjuśrī into the chamber, the śrāvakas all abandoned the Lesser Vehicle and aspired to the Greater Vehicle.
Those others who dwell in other gardens were made to submit by Ānanda’s censure here;
they likewise all abandoned their minor aspirations and yearned for the Great [Vehicle], deeply resolving their minds toward omniscience.
That is to say, his aspiration is so profound that he does not allow himself to retreat or forget his purpose halfway;
furthermore, even when encountering the afflictions of sensual pleasures, he does not suddenly retreat or become deluded upon seeing those who come to him with requests.
Seeking the Dharma causes my benefit of the Dharma to increase daily;
seeking wealth causes my mind of renunciation to become ever more expansive.
This is truly a virtuous teacher who promotes my progress toward the benefits of the Path. Thus, I relinquish all that I possess.
The commentary states:
"That the sublime aspiration has its locus is precisely what is 'great.
This is the fruit of omniscience."
Regarding the emptiness of cause and effect:
if one examines the cause of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), it will necessarily reach the fruit of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). As for the various perfections (*pāramitās*):
The previous section spoke separately of generosity and ethical discipline;
the present mention of "all the pāramitās" refers to the remaining four perfections. Regarding "accomplishing one's own buddha-field":
This means that by cultivating the causes for those Tathāgatas' practices and vows, one likewise adorns one's own land with the same adornments as those Tathāgatas.
As stated in the "Chapter on Seeing Akṣobhya Buddha" in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra*: [text follows].
Regarding the title "Chapter on Seeing the Tathāgata": according to the first half of the chapter, it should be titled "Seeing the Tathāgata";
according to the second half of the chapter, it should be titled "Seeing Akṣobhya.
There is no difference in meaning between them. As for the question, "By what marks does one contemplate the Tathāgata?"—
The True Vehicle of the Mahāyāna leaves behind appearances and is free from attachment;
yet those who listen and seek all grasp at signs to give rise to faith.
Therefore, in the aforementioned [sūtra], Mañjuśrī entered Vimalakīrti’s room, which was empty, to await him.
In the "Chapter on the Inconceivable," Śāriputra seeks a seat from Vimalakīrti,
who instructs him by sending him out to seek one.
Now these two great beings are returning to the garden, just as they are about to see the Buddha.
However, most of those who listen are attached to marks and seek a true substratum upon which to base their faith. Therefore,
he asks them about what they have come to observe,
so that they may describe the mark of its non-existence and thereby attain awakening.
Mañjuśrī entered the room and came without the appearance of coming;
Vimalakīrti saw the Buddha and saw him without the appearance of seeing;
Śāriputra sought the Dharma and sought it with a mind that had severed all seeking.
"Maitreya attains the prediction apart from attaining it" means that he attains it by being free from the prediction.
"Exquisite and transcending the ordinary realm" refers to the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), which constitute the ordinary realm;
because the Tathāgata is both form and non-form, it is said to be "exquisite and transcendent. "Then, the true" refers to those who are identical with the True.
This means that the Pure Name (Vimalakīrti), having attained awakening, perceives the Buddha as formless by dispelling the perception of self-characteristics.

Those who falsely claim to share this same dharma are likewise unawakened; they cling to their own bodies as having substantial existence and thus see the body of the Tathāgata as possessing form—this is also the same.
Thus, holding both is called a shared failure;
letting go of both is called a shared attainment. "Neither this nor that" means that the essence of "this" and "that" is empty.
"Not by this and not by that" [means that neither is the cause].

"By means of" refers to the mind not being attached to using this or that. "Not abiding in directions" clarifies that the Dharmakāya does not abide exclusively in any particular direction. "Not departing from directions" [means...]
Pervading all places, he is equal to all wise ones;
supreme above the supreme, he is identical to sentient beings,
yet below there is no lower.
Observing by means of this, one departs from the aforementioned hundred negations;
therefore, it is called right view.
If one observes otherwise, it is identical to the aforementioned hundred negations and is thus termed wrong. This is what Śāriputra asked of Vimalakīrti.
The two venerable ones, Śāriputra and Kāśyapa, were sites for the traces of the śrāvakas who, having been guided from the Small Vehicle toward the Great,
thus, from the beginning of the assembly, either posed questions by feigning delusion or expressed sorrowful repentance under the guise of awakening.
These are all instances of the Bodhisattva’s skillful means (upāya) in exhorting others to reach the ultimate goal.
What are these matters? They are as described in the "Chapter on the Buddha-land" (Buddhakṣetraparivarta).
Since the two questions had not yet been answered and the assembly remained unenlightened,
Śāriputra provisionally took up the effect to inquire about the cause, thereby causing the assembly to attain awakening.
Mañjuśrī entered the room to inquire after his illness;
the empty room and lack of attendants symbolized that the Buddha-fields are likewise entirely empty.
In the "Inconceivable" chapter, Śāriputra, through a provisional thought regarding the couch, initiated the conditions for the state of non-seeking.
By borrowing the seat, he clarifies the function of inconceivable liberation.
Furthermore, Śāriputra and Kāśyapa, having received the essential meaning, lamented their own [limitations],
thereby clarifying that all śrāvakas ought to wail, while the three thousand bodhisattvas rejoice and receive this Dharma upon the crown of their heads.

Chapter on Contemplating Sentient Beings, Part Two: The Two Great Beings discuss that the nature of sentient beings is empty—that is, true emptiness—which is fully endowed with kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity.
This is occasioned by the scattering of flowers by the goddesses and Śāriputra’s response thereto.
This extensively clarifies the difference between the two types of functional power: the conceivable liberation and the inconceivable liberation.
In the "Chapter on the Buddha-Way," the two Great Beings extensively clarify how those who do not practice the Way nonetheless proceed upon the Buddha-way.
Śāriputra Kāśyapa, demonstrating that he was still within the realm of the unattained, sighed and expressed his realization, saying:
"Ordinary beings [strive] for Buddhahood, while Śrāvakas have none;
countless Śrāvakas have turned their minds toward the Great Vehicle, deprecating the Lesser Vehicle."
The "Chapter on Fragrant Accumulation" clarifies that the dharma-gates of the two lands— the pure and the defiled— are different.
Śāriputra ate the Buddha’s remaining food,
and upon reaching the "Chapter on Bodhisattvas," he spoke to the Buddha of his own accord.
This was not something conceived by my mind nor measured by my judgment;
furthermore, I relied on Ānanda to suppress my transgressions.
From this day forward, I dare not call myself one of great learning.
He immediately caused countless śrāvakas to abandon their lesser aspirations and rejoice in the Great [Vehicle].
Within this context, he further provisionally inquired about Vimalakīrti’s passing and rebirth;
now, he personally declares the application of the dharma-body.
Neither passing away nor being born, he was able to manifest both death and birth,
causing countless sentient beings to resolve their minds on Bodhisattvahood and vow to be reborn in the Pure Land.
All the aforementioned accounts illustrate how Mañjuśrī, the one of sublime renown, likewise subdued those two great Śrāvakas of inferior capacity.
By these skillful means, he leads innumerable practitioners of the provisional methods of the Hīnayāna;
some realize the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) on that very seat,
while others attain the patience of non-arising only upon reaching the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, or the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* sūtras.
Although there are distinctions of superiority and inferiority in their descriptions, the efficacy of their transformative power is one and the same.
As for the question, "From where did you pass away to come here?"— the reason for this exchange is that it establishes the meaning of the preceding [teaching on] both form and formlessness.
Those who are deluded claim that there is a principle distinct from phenomena and a dharma-body distinct from the response-body (nirmāṇakāya).
Therefore, the purpose of this dialogue is to let them know that birth is non-birth and that marks are markless.
Furthermore, the previous horizontal refutation of the hundred fallacies is called "horizontal pervasion" (heng-bian).

This present [refutation] is "vertical enumeration" (shu-die), which is both pervasive and profound. It is pervasive because it addresses the very moment of arising and ceasing; it is profound because it penetrates the depths of existence.
The principle of the Dharmakāya is perfected. As for "when the sunlight appears," this clarifies the Nirmāṇakāya.
Since it was previously established that birth and non-birth are identical as the True Body (Svabhāvakāya), [the appearance of the sun now signifies its manifestation].
This clarifies that which is unborn yet arises, thereby distinguishing the *saṃbhogakāya*.
Furthermore, just as sunlight is inherently luminous and cannot be obscured,
this metaphor illustrates that the original enlightenment (*mūlajñāna*) of the *dharmakāya* remains unaffected by defilement even while dwelling within it.
"Capable of destroying all darkness" is a metaphor for the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body),
which responds to sentient beings by turning them back from delusion toward awakening. "Trāyastriṃśa" is a term in the Sanskrit language (*Brahma-svara*).
This refers to the Heaven of the Thirty-three. "Akaniṣṭha" is a Sanskrit term;
it is translated here as the Heaven of Ultimate Form (Akaniṣṭha-bhavana).
This refers to the summit of the heavens of the Form Realm (rūpadhātu).
Regarding the "Chapter on Dharma-Offering," "Dharma" refers to the Dharma of the Middle Way and True Reality (bhūtatathatā) within the Mahāyāna.
Therefore, the text says:
These are the profound sūtras spoken by all Buddhas.
Regarding "making offerings," there are two kinds of texts.
The first is to recite and study [the scriptures] for liberation; this is called shallow.
The second is to practice according to the teaching and attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); this is called deep.
If one follows the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*:
Offerings of flower fragrances, necklaces, and the transcription [of the text], as well as rejoicing [in its merit], are all dharma-offerings.
Question:
Are these offerings made to the Buddha, or are they offerings made to the Dharma?
Answer: Because one makes offerings to the Buddha with a mind that protects and upholds the True Dharma.
Thus, the text says:
"To uphold, recite, and make offerings to this sutra is to make offerings to the Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
Furthermore, at the conclusion of the chapter, the exhortation states:
Therefore, O Lord of Devas, you should honor the Buddha with the offering of the Dharma.

These two chapters belong to the section on the dissemination [of the teaching]; in this chapter, the true and great benefits of the Dharma are first praised, and the audience is exhorted to make offerings.
In a later chapter, one may then diligently and exhaustively entrust him with the propagation [of the teaching].
"Hundred thousand sūtras" refers to the *Āgama* sūtras of the Hīnayāna. "Mastery of supernatural powers" (ṛddhi-vaśitā) refers to...
This praises the power and function of realization.

This refers to the bodily relics (śarīra), which may be whole or fragmented;
the present mention of "whole" indicates that their merit is greater. As for the "jewel stupa" (ratnastūpa):
It should be stated as "Huazhe" (化身); it appears in various sutras and śāstras as either "Shusou" (叔藪) or "Piji" (彼),
or as "Huatapo" (化塔婆).
It is also called *tōba*, or *tōba*,
or referred to as *sūtōba*.
Some call it *zhidi fudu*, also rendered as *zhiti futu*;
in the new terminology, it is called *sudupo*.
This is translated as "temple" (*miao*).

It is first of all a representation of the honored ancestors."
The character 薨 (hóng) is glossed as "cloud.
A *tá* (stūpa) is a Buddhist hall. The characters for "pagoda spire" (*biǎo chà*) are also written as 𢲉;
they share the same pronunciation.
Examining the Sanskrit sound,
it is sometimes called *cātur*,
which translates as "land" or "field."
Regarding the phrase "or acts as a kṣetra," it preserves two pronunciations; one should instead say "to set up a pole" (li zhān).

*Kṣatriya* is translated here as "Black" (*kṛṣṇa*),

The Great Sūtra states:
"All World-Honored Ones come from the six pāramitās, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and the eleven [auxiliaries] to reach Great Nirvāṇa.

the Great Sūtra states:

The Mahāyāna Sūtra states:

"Not abandoning the original resolve for enlightenment constitutes attaining Great Nirvāṇa; this is called non-retrogression. Sixth is "World-Knower," a title signifying the perfect clarity of expedient wisdom.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Knowing the world" (*lokavid*) means simply knowing.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
He thoroughly knows all categories of the defiled and purified characteristics of the world-realm and the realm of sentient beings.
Seventh, he is a Supreme Being who transcends the titles of all worthy sages.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra states:
"The Tathāgata is truly neither a *puruṣa* nor a non-*puruṣa*; he is called a *puruṣa* because he disciplines *puruṣas*.
These two titles are distinguished as two according to the Mahāyāna Sūtra.

"The Unsurpassed Great Man,
the Teacher of the Nine Heavens and Humans."
He is called the One Who Skillfully Guides Sentient Beings.
As the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:
"Because he has truly been a teacher of the Dharma-realm for gods and humans many times in the past," it is so called.
The tenth is the title "Victorious Awakening of the Teacherless Buddha.
This clarifies that he is self-awakened without a teacher, such that no delusions can obscure him.

According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the World-Honored One’s ten titles are external designations. He possesses the seven treasures, a thousand sons, and is a prince of the golden wheel-turning monarch.
First, the wheel-treasure;
second, the jewel-treasure;
third, the woman-treasure.
Fourth, the precious elephant;
fifth, the precious horse;
sixth, the precious minister of the treasury.
Regarding the seventh, the Treasure of the Military Minister, that which is sealed with the *dhāraṇī* seal:
the treatise states that the Hīnayāna sūtras contain the three seals of the Dharma (*tridharmamudrā*).
That is to say, [the teachings on] impermanence, suffering,
and non-self are sealed by the Mahāyāna’s seal of the single jewel-mark;
thus one is able to skillfully discern the characteristics of all phenomena.
It is unmoving within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*),
such that neither the four propositions nor the hundred negations can shake it.
That which is sealed by this seal is entirely the Perfect and Sudden Mahāyāna.
The "Chapter on the Pure Dhāraṇī" in the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra* states:
"One seals all phenomena with the seal of space;
by means of the seal of signlessness, one is able to manifest that space as signless."
Furthermore, a verse says:
"The Buddhas possess nothing;
they are neither born nor do they die."
There is nothing that exists which can be grasped.
How, then, can it be universally maintained?
If one can understand all things in this way according to principle, [one attains universal maintenance].
That which is without conceptual discrimination is able to achieve universal retention. "Decisively being without self" refers to the emptiness of the person (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
"Being free from 'mine' due to causes, conditions, and karmic retribution" refers to the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). As for the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*):
Regarding the words in the thirty-ninth chapter of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*:

"Speaking of birth and death" means knowing that birth and death have no abiding. "Speaking of the flavor of nirvāṇa" means knowing that nirvāṇa is without speech. "Speaking of the various vehicles (*yāna*) as the place where the mind finds rest" means knowing that all vehicles enter the gateway of the wisdom of the single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇajñāna*). "Speaking of the cultivation and accumulation of extensive and magnificent merits from the initial resolve until sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*)" means that in a single thought-moment, wisdom awakens to all phenomena.
To state the essentials:

being able to expound the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma is called speech; knowing that all written characters are inexpressible is called [wisdom]. Furthermore, "consciousness" refers to the consciousness of the four great elements.
The wise person dwells in the four great elements as being without intrinsic nature.
The cognizer cognizes the six sense organs and the six consciousnesses.
The wise person is tranquil both internally and externally.
The same applies to arising and non-arising, grasping and non-grasping, having an object of perception and lacking an object of perception.

Furthermore, it is not understood that the sūtras speak of the suffering and affliction of saṃsāra; it is not understood that they speak of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa as being of one single characteristic; nor is it understood that they speak of the self, persons, and all phenomena for those who have realized [the truth].
It is said that there are three kinds of emptiness and selflessness.
Furthermore, "person" (pudgala) refers to grasping at the view of a person;
"dharma" refers to understanding the absence of a person and the absence of views.
"Person" refers to ordinary beings, sages, and those of the three vehicles. "Dharma" refers to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
One definitively knows that all dharmas are without distinction or difference, like empty space, and no longer gives rise to views.
The commentary states:

"Observing above that causes and conditions are impermanent and without self" refers to the aforementioned gate of attaining the patience of non-arising by being free from all false views. "Attaining the patience of docility" [is explained as follows].

In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the three types of patience (*kṣānti*) are as follows: the patience of subduing through dry wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā-vinaya-kṣānti*) pertains to the outer ordinary beings (*bāhyapṛthagjana*); the patience of conformity (*anuloma-kṣānti*) pertains to the inner ordinary beings (*antarapṛthagjana*), specifically those from the stage of the eight persons (*aṣṭamaka*) onward; and that which is beyond this is called the patience of non-arising (*anutpāda-kṣānti*).
Although these three vehicles share the same practice, [they differ in their realization].
The followers of the two vehicles do not receive the name of "patience" (kṣānti) when they attain realization;
because the bodhisattva does not [prematurely] realize [the ultimate], he receives the name of patience.
If one follows the *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra):
The thirty stages prior to the Grounds within the Dharma-gate of the Five Patiences are collectively termed the Patience of Subduing (伏忍).
The first, second, and third grounds constitute the Patience of Faith (信忍);
the fourth, fifth, and sixth grounds constitute the Patience of Accordance (順忍).
The seventh, eighth, and ninth stages consist of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);
the tenth stage and the fruit of Buddhahood consist of the patience of cessation (*nirodha-kṣānti*).
Now, according to the *Ratnaketuparipṛcchā-sūtra*, upon entering the fourth stage, one attains the five supernormal powers (*pañca-abhijñā*) and the functional application of bodily karma.
The function of mental karma through the attainment of dhāraṇī,
and the function of vocal karma through eloquence—
these three constitute the sublime gateways for the purpose of transforming sentient beings.
Because he is the true treasury where the accumulated roots of wholesome karma are stored, he is designated separately. Kālakaraṇḍa is also called Krakucchanda;
he is the fourth Buddha among the Seven Buddhas.
He is the foremost of the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa.
Loushi is also called Luzhi;
this translates as "Weeping."
This means that when the first thousand people set forth on the path, they all immediately attained Buddhahood and saved sentient beings;
only when Loushi (Ruci) finally attained Buddhahood did he say,
"All those who previously attained the Way have already saved all sentient beings."
"I weep and shed tears, wondering what I shall deliver when I later attain the Way.
The Imperial Edict for the Dharma Master’s Verse says:
"In this present Bhadrakalpa..."
Precisely at the ninth moment of cessation,
within this process of increase and decrease,
there are the four [stages] beginning with *kṛta*.
When the lifespan was sixty-four thousand years,
a Muni appeared at the age of one hundred;
[this occurred] when it had decreased to the third ten-thousand-year period.
Famine shall arise at that time;
twenty times ten armies [shall wage war],
and sons shall be eight times ten thousand times the number of their fathers.
During one period of increase and decrease,
Maitreya shall arise next; from this point,
it will be the tenth eon of destruction.
Up to the fifteenth extinction,
within that single cycle of increase and decrease,
there are nine hundred and ninety-four [aeons].
The Great Sages arise in succession.
Regarding what is called the "Auspicious Aeon" (Bhadrakalpa):
at the beginning of this aeon, a thousand-petaled lotus appeared upon the water.
The devas all exclaimed, "Excellent!
In this kalpa, one thousand worthies shall appear in the world.
For this reason, it was thus named.
The Chapter on Entrustment. In the preceding chapter, the true and great benefits of the Dharma were praised;
therefore, in this chapter, there is a fervent entrustment.

Regarding the two dharmas for those newly learning: first is disparaging the Dharma, and second is being arrogant toward the teacher. To revere the teacher is to respect the Dharma; to honor the Dharma is to practice it.
If one practices accordingly, one immediately severs delusions and becomes a sage. By this reasoning,
although it is said that one honors the teacher, it is in fact the realization of self-honor.
Yet those who are newly learned disparage their teachers and treat the Dharma with contempt, thereby blocking the path toward progress and inquiry for themselves.
They first practice two things:
the first is deceiving others.
Second is the method of subterfuge:
by exhausting the activities of those newly initiated into the stages of benefit, one may achieve success;
by focusing exclusively on the true nature of reality, the merit of self-liberation will be realized.
How regrettable that you slight others and fail in compassion and kindness, and that your falsehoods obstruct your true vision!
Yet these admonitions are most earnest;
may all who aspire to advancement take them to heart and engrave them within their very marrow.
